Lecture 1: Introduction to Distributed Systems

Source: Lecture1.pdf, slides 1–24

Why distributed systems matter

The lecture opens with systems you already use daily: mobile telephone networks, the Internet and its many protocols, banking and reservation systems, and ride-hailing systems such as Uber or Ola. The common thread is that no single machine holds all the data or makes all the decisions.

Distributed system (slide 9) A collection of N independent processes that communicate with each other either through a shared medium or by exchanging messages. The data is usually not at one location. Each site (processor, node) makes local decisions based on its own data, its own computation, and the messages it receives.

Evolution in four generations

The slides trace how the style of distributed systems changed. Read these as a timeline with three properties that moved over time: how much central control there is, how large the scale is, and how rich the features are.

  • First generation: email and bulletin board systems, early Internet services, and file systems such as AFS and NFS. These relied heavily on Remote Procedure Calls (RPC).
  • Second generation (from the late 1990s): grid computing and peer-to-peer file sharing (Gnutella, Napster, and others). These brought more sophisticated resource sharing.
  • Third generation: large-scale cloud facilities and virtualization, stream processing, and blockchain systems.
  • Fourth generation: integration of many systems, interoperability, cross-system protocols and security, and heterogeneity.

The slides summarise the trend this way. Early systems had more central control. Grid systems still need a little central control. Fully distributed systems need none. Scale and feature richness grow from generation to generation.

The basic computation model

Each process runs locally and sees only its own state and the messages that reach it. There is no global view by default. Most of the difficulty in the rest of the course comes from this one fact. Variations of the model are also listed, and the slides point out that there are almost as many models as researchers. The main axes are:

  • Synchronous or asynchronous communication.
  • Message size: limited or unlimited.
  • What local computation is allowed.
  • Message delivery order: FIFO, arbitrary, or causal.
  • Blocking versus non-blocking communication.
  • Fault-free systems versus systems with faults, and the type of fault.

High-level challenges

The slides use a series of concrete problems to motivate the course. Each one points to a later topic.

  • Time. How do we measure time accurately, and how do computers keep time? The SI second is defined by 9,192,631,770 transitions of the caesium-133 atom (background: this is the standard definition). Computers, however, use quartz crystal oscillations, where one second is 32,768 oscillations. Quartz clocks drift, partly because of ambient heat, so physically separated computers need clock synchronization. This leads to Lectures 2 and 3.
  • Content delivery. Serving video and images on the Internet needs strong caching and search models. Real-time video is hard. Content can be reused, so it need not always come from the source. This makes locality and replication important.
  • Replication and consistency. Copies of data must agree.
  • Banking. Until the 1990s, accounts were kept locally and branches tallied balances in end-of-day batches. From the early 2000s, CORE banking (Centralized Online Real-time Exchange) connected branches on shared software. Today, UPI moves money through mobile apps. The hard requirement is correct operation of accounts under failures. A transfer between two banks updates databases at different locations in different administrative domains.
  • Programming. Programmers need suitable abstractions, with or without shared memory. Programs must cope with a lot of uncertainty. Verification and debugging get harder, and one useful tactic is to replay the same event sequence.
  • Large data. Data is partitioned across machines. This raises three questions: how to store the data, how to search it quickly and at scale, and how to keep the coding efficient.

Where distributed systems sit in computer science

The slides list the areas that the topic cuts across: programming frameworks and APIs; data structures such as hash tables; algorithms for routing and search; databases with distributed transactions; operating systems (resource management, mutual exclusion, file systems); applications such as the Internet, CDNs, the Google File System, and Bitcoin; security (authentication, confidentiality, non-repudiation, availability, and denial of service); and software engineering (distributed verification and debugging).

Course structure and policies

The syllabus has five modules. Module 1 covers introduction, communication models, time and synchronization, and practice with MPI and MapReduce. Module 2 covers distributed file systems, consensus, agreement and locking, and practice with GFS and Chubby. Module 3 covers distributed databases and practice with NoSQL and MongoDB. Module 4 covers limitations of distributed computing, self-stabilization, and the CAP theorem. Module 5 covers distributed algorithms for graphs and guest lectures. The syllabus is marked tentative.

Grading (tentative): scheduled and unscheduled quizzes 20% (no makeups, and no allowance for unscheduled in-class exams), mid exam 20%, homeworks 15%, project 20%, final exam 25%. Homeworks include hand-written and programming parts, and some are group-based. Copying is strictly prohibited, and the first violation gets a direct zero. The first homework is to read one of the posted papers in detail and write a short report covering what the result is, its main result, its significance, why it is useful, what is interesting about it, and how it could be improved.

Exam pointers:
  • The four generations of distributed systems, and how central control, scale, and features change across them.
  • The definition of a distributed system as N independent processes that communicate by shared medium or messages, with local decisions only.
  • Why clocks drift (quartz oscillation, heat), and why this creates the clock synchronization problem.
  • The grading weights: quizzes 20, mid 20, homeworks 15, project 20, final 25.

Lecture 2: Physical Time and Synchronization

Source: Lecture2.pdf, slides 1–37

Why processes need the time

On a single computer, there is one clock. A process asks the kernel for the time with a system call, and that answer is "the time". In a distributed system there is no global clock and no shared memory. Each processor has its own clock and its own notion of time. Clocks drift, so they can gain or lose seconds per day, and clocks that start synchronized will tick at different rates and fall apart. Applications need a shared notion of time for many reasons: timestamping events, detecting events with timeouts, measuring performance and resource usage, and making scheduling decisions.

Clock vocabulary

The slides define the terms you need for exam questions. Let Ca(t) be a clock and t real (UTC) time.

  • Perfect clock: Ca(t) = t at all times.
  • Offset: Ca(t) − t. The offset of Ca relative to Cb at time t is Ca(t) − Cb(t).
  • Skew: Fa(t) − Ft, where Fa = 1/Ca and Ft = 1/t (F stands for frequency). Skew between two clocks is Fa(t) − Fb(t).
  • Drift: the slides define it as the second derivative of Ca.
  • Accuracy: for a threshold ρ, a clock is accurate if 1 − ρ ≤ dC/dt ≤ 1 + ρ. (The symbol for the threshold is lost in the slide text. ρ is the usual choice, background.)

Network time protocols

Before discussing distributed clocks, the slides look at networked systems. The first protocol was by Gusella and Zatti (1983), and it was used in BSD 4.3 as the adjtime() system call.

Gusella and Zatti (TEMPO)

Take two machines A and B. A sends a timestamped message to B. B replies, and A records the reply. Let T1 be the one-way transmission delay and the offset be the quantity being estimated. The two exchanges give:

  • D1 = tB − eB − tA + eA = T1 + (offset) − Error1. (The offset symbol is lost in the slide text. e is the error in each clock's reading.)
  • D2 = tA2 − tB2 − (eA2 − eB2) = T2 − (offset) − Error2 for the reply.
  • A computes θ′ = (D1 − D2)/2 = (offset) + (T1 − T2)/2 − (Error1 − Error2)/2. If the two one-way delays are roughly equal, the delay terms cancel and θ′ is a good estimate of the offset.

TEMPO extends this to a LAN. One computer is the master and the others are slaves. The master:

  1. Interacts with each slave S1, S2, … and gets an estimate Δ′Si for each one.
  2. Computes the average of all the Δ′Si values as the network average error.
  3. Tells each slave Si to adjust its clock by the difference between Δ′Si and that average.

Worked example from the figure. The four estimates are +30, −10, +15 and −20 seconds. Their average is 15/4 = 3.75 s. The slides do not work this through, so the exact adjustment for each slave depends on the sign convention. Read the wording literally: slave Si is told to adjust by Δ′Si minus the average. For S1 that is 30 − 3.75 = 26.25 s.

A catch is noted on slide 18. Some slaves must move their clock backwards into the past. The adjtime() call handles this by changing the rate at which the clock runs, not by jumping. This can avoid a visible jump, but the result is not always consistent with the clock behaving as expected.

NTP: Network Time Protocol

NTP lets systems on a common network, such as the Internet, synchronize time up to some error. The model has clients and servers. Clients get the current time from a server on the network. Servers form a hierarchy (strata) that can go as deep as 15 levels. A server gets its time either from one or more servers one level up, or from peers at the same level.

Synchronizing once is not enough, because clocks drift in unpredictable directions. Peers therefore exchange messages periodically. NTP was designed by David Mills of the University of Delaware, who died in January 2024.

Offset estimation between two peers

The idea is to run several trials and keep the trial with the minimum delay. Each trial uses four timestamps, T1 to T4. Let a = T1 − T3 and b = T2 − T4. If the differential delay (the difference between the A-to-B and B-to-A delays) is small, then:

  • Offset θ = (a + b)/2
  • Round-trip delay = a − b = T1 − T3 + T4 − T2

The slides justify these by adding T1 = T3 + (delay) + θ and T2 = T4 − (delay) + θ, which gives 2θ = a + b.

The slide 30 version uses a different notation: A's clock is A(t) = B(t) + O, and the timestamps are T(i−3), T(i−2), T(i−1) and T(i). Then:

  • Offset Oi = (Ti−2 − Ti−3 + Ti−1 − Ti) / 2
  • Round-trip delay Di = (Ti − Ti−3) − (Ti−1 − Ti−2)

Each peer keeps the eight most recent pairs (Oi, Di). The offset that goes with the minimum Di is the one used as the estimate of O.

After the offset: the rest of NTP

Estimating the offset is only one part of NTP. The protocol must also decide how to reset the time using the offset, how to choose peers and remove bad ones, how to handle temporary glitches, and how to tolerate faults. The slides mention these but do not explain them in detail.

Why NTP does not suffice for distributed systems

  • In a distributed system, there is no way to arrange the NTP strata neatly.
  • Typical NTP accuracy is in the order of milliseconds. On a bad day, errors reach hundreds of milliseconds. A LAN can do better than 1 ms.
  • Clock synchronization needs peering support that large deployments may not have.

The slides point to a simulation of time synchronization on the Virtual Labs site (search for Distributed Systems-I, then the Time experiment).

Global-scale approaches: TrueTime and other systems

Companies such as Google, Facebook and Amazon run planet-scale services and need good time synchronization. The slides say their answer is engineering rather than the NTP model.

TrueTime (slides 35–36) puts one or more TimeMaster servers in each datacenter. There are two kinds:

  • GPS TimeMasters have GPS receivers that get time from satellites.
  • Armageddon TimeMasters have atomic clocks.

The two kinds are deliberately different. Their failures are independent, so using both gives redundancy. TimeMasters compare their times with each other over a dedicated, fault-tolerant, high-speed fabric. A client pings a set of TimeMasters of both kinds across the network. (Background: TrueTime is the time API used by Google's Spanner database.)

Other systems mentioned: Amazon's TimeSync, which is also based on GPS and atomic clocks, and chrony, which the slides attribute to Facebook.

Exam pointers:
  • The Gusella–Zatti estimate: D1 and D2 for the two directions, and θ′ = (D1 − D2)/2 with the delays cancelling when they are roughly equal. Know the TEMPO steps: average the Δ′Si, then adjust each slave by Δ′Si minus the average.
  • NTP offset and delay: a = T1 − T3, b = T2 − T4, θ = (a + b)/2, round-trip = a − b. Also the Oi and Di form used on slide 30, and the rule of picking the minimum-delay pair from the eight most recent.
  • Offset, skew and drift are different quantities. Be ready to define each one.
  • Why NTP is not enough at scale (ms accuracy, hierarchy, peering), and what TrueTime changes (GPS plus atomic clocks, independent failure modes).

Lecture 3: Logical Time (Causality, Scalar and Vector Clocks)

Source: Lecture3.pdf, slides 1–49

Why logical time

Physical clocks are expensive to keep synchronized, and NTP is not a good fit for most distributed systems. Asynchronous computations still make progress in spurts, so what matters for most systems is the order of events, not their exact wall-clock times. Logical time captures the monotonicity of causality: if one event could have affected another, it gets an earlier timestamp. Causality is useful for designing distributed algorithms, tracking dependent events, knowing how far a computation has progressed, and measuring concurrency.

Modelling a distributed computation

A distributed system is a set of processors plus a communication network. Processors can fail and share no global memory. The network has finite but unpredictable delays. Messages may be reordered, lost, garbled, or duplicated. Links can become unavailable.

A distributed program has n processes P1 … Pn, typically one per processor, and a channel Cij from Pi to Pj. The state of a process is its local memory plus the context of the messages it has sent and received. The state of a channel is the set of messages in transit on it.

The execution is made of three kinds of events:

  • Local (internal) action: changes the state of the process where it happens.
  • Send, send(m): changes the state of the sender and the state of the channel carrying m.
  • Receive, recv(m): changes the state of the receiver and the state of the channel m arrived on.

Sending is non-blocking, so the sender does not wait for delivery. Local actions are spontaneous. Ei is the set of events at process Pi, and the local order on Ei is written →i. The events at one process are totally ordered, and that order is the local causal dependency. For messages, send(m) →msg recv(m) for every message m.

The happened-before relation

The relation → across all events E is defined by three rules. Event ex_i → ey_j if any of these holds:

  1. i = j and x < y (same process, earlier event), or
  2. ex_i →msg ey_j (a message is sent at ex_i and received at ey_j), or
  3. there is some ez_k with ex_i → ez_k and ez_k → ey_j (transitivity).

Notation used on the slides: ex_i means the x-th event at process Pi. So e^4_2 is the fourth event at P2.

Logical concurrency

Two events are logically concurrent, written ei || ej, when neither causally affects the other: not(ei → ej) and not(ej → ei). Concurrent events need not happen at the same physical time. They just cannot have influenced each other.

Using this figure, the slides give these examples:

  • Concurrent: e^4_2 and e^3_3; e^1_3 and e^3_1; e^4_2 and e^1_3.
  • Causal: e^3_3 → e^5_1 (e^3_3 comes before the send e^4_3, which is received at e^4_1, which comes before e^5_1); e^2_1 → e^3_2 (the send e^2_1 is received at e^2_2, which comes before e^3_2 in the same process); e^4_3 → e^5_1.

Logical clocks: the general framework

A logical clock system has a time domain T and a logical clock C that maps each event to a timestamp C(e) in T. T is partially ordered under a relation <, which is the analogue of "earlier than" for physical time. The required property is the clock consistency condition:

e_i → e_j ⇒ C(e_i) < C(e_j)

A clock system that also satisfies the converse, C(e_i) < C(e_j) ⇒ e_i → e_j, is strongly consistent. This is the property scalar time lacks.

Each process keeps two data structures: a local logical clock lci that measures its own progress, and a global logical clock gci that is its view of global progress (lci is usually part of gci). Each process needs two rules:

  • Rule 1: how the local clock updates when an event happens.
  • Rule 2: how the process updates its global view when it receives a message.

Systems differ in how they represent time and in their update protocols. All of them follow Rules 1 and 2 to keep causality monotone.

Scalar time (Lamport, 1978)

Lamport proposed scalar time in 1978. He won the 2013 Turing Award, in part for the concepts of causality and logical clocks. The time domain is the non-negative integers. Each process has one integer Ci that serves both as its local clock and as its view of global time.

  • Rule 1: before any event (send, receive or internal), Ci := Ci + d, with d > 0. Usually d = 1.
  • Rule 2: each message carries the sender's clock value Cmsg. When Pi receives it: (1) Ci := max(Ci, Cmsg); (2) execute Rule 1; (3) deliver the message.

Worked example from the figure. The scalar timestamps in the four-process figure (slide 27) are:

  • P1: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The third event is a receive of the message sent with timestamp 2 by P2, so 3 = max(2, 2) + 1.
  • P2: 1, 2, 4. The fourth event is a receive of a message sent with timestamp 3 by P3, so 4 = max(2, 3) + 1.
  • P3: 1, 2, 3, 5. The fifth event receives a message sent with timestamp 4 by P4, so 5 = max(3, 4) + 1.
  • P4: 1, 3, 4. The second event receives a message sent with timestamp 2 by P3, so 3 = max(1, 2) + 1.

Properties of scalar time

  • Monotonicity: e_i → e_j implies C(e_i) < C(e_j).
  • Total order: timestamps alone do not give a total order, because two events on different processes can have the same timestamp. Use the pair (t, i) and compare t first, then the process id i. This gives a total order consistent with →.
  • Event counting: with d = 1, an event with timestamp t depends on t − 1 earlier events. This is called the height of the event.
  • Not strongly consistent. The slides give a counterexample: the fifth event at p1 has scalar timestamp 5, and the third event at p4 has timestamp 4 in the scalar figure. Since 5 > 4, one might think p1's fifth event came after p4's third. It did not. The vector clocks below show these two events are concurrent.

Vector time

Scalar time loses causality across processes because one number serves as both local clock and global view. Vector time fixes this, at the cost of bigger timestamps. Time is an n-dimensional vector of non-negative integers. Process Pi keeps vti[1..n]. vti[i] is its own logical clock, and vti[j] is its latest knowledge of Pj's local time. The whole vector is Pi's view of global logical time, and the timestamp of an event is the vector at the moment it executes.

  • Rule 1: before an event, vti[i] := vti[i] + d (d > 0).
  • Rule 2: each message m carries the sender's vector vt. On receipt: for every k, vti[k] := max(vti[k], vt[k]); then execute Rule 1; then deliver m.

Comparing vector timestamps

  • vh = vk iff vh[i] = vk[i] for all i.
  • vh ≤ vk iff vh[i] ≤ vk[i] for all i.
  • vh < vk iff vh ≤ vk and there is some i with vh[i] < vk[i].
  • vh || vk (concurrent) iff neither vh < vk nor vk < vh.

Slide examples: [1, 3, 4] < [1, 5, 6]. [2, 5, 3] and [3, 4, 4] are concurrent, because the first is smaller in component 1 and larger in component 2.

In the same figure, the fifth event of P1 is [5, 2, 0, 0] and the third event of P4 is [0, 0, 2, 3]. Neither vector is ≤ the other, so these events are concurrent. This is the counterexample that scalar time could not resolve.

Properties of vector time

  • Event counting: with d = 1, vti[i] is the number of events that have occurred at Pi so far. If an event e has timestamp vh, then vh[j] is the number of events at Pj that causally precede e. The total number of events that causally precede e is (Σj vh[j]) − 1.
  • Strong consistency: vector clocks are strongly consistent. For any two events, you can decide from their timestamps whether they are causally related. The slides leave the proof as an exercise.

Limitations of vector time

  • Each message carries the whole vector, so message size grows linearly with the number of processes. With thousands of processes, even a few events produce large messages.
  • The slides mention that few techniques exist to reduce this overhead.

Optimization: send only the changed entries

Between two messages from Pi to Pj, only some vector components change. So Pi can send just the tuples (i1, t1), (i2, t2), …, and Pj updates component k to max(vtj[k], tk). Message size drops in general. The catch is local storage: Pi has to remember, for each j, the vector it had when it last sent to Pj. That is O(n²) storage. A clever trick brings this down to O(n). The slides refer to the Kshemkalyani and Singhal book for it.

Where vector clocks are used

The slides list Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, distributed logging, and GFS and HDFS. In all of them, tracking the order of events and understanding causality is critical.

Beyond vector time and the limits of logical time

  • Matrix time (Wu and Bernstein) uses more elaborate logical clocks. The slides point to the book for details.
  • Scalar time is cheap but not strongly consistent. Vector and matrix time are strongly consistent but have large overheads that grow with system size.
  • Logical time assumes all interactions happen inside the system. Cyber-physical systems (CPS) and IoT break this assumption, because they interact through physical channels too.
  • There is little room for error handling.

Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) combine logical and physical time. Physical time usually orders events across nodes, but tight synchronization is expensive, and within the window of uncertainty physical time is not enough. HLC uses logical clocks only to resolve ties inside that window, and physical time otherwise. The slides call it the best of both worlds and refer to the book for details.

Practice: Virtual Lab

Scalar and vector clocks are also available as simulations on the Virtual Labs site (vlabs.co.in, search for Distributed Systems). Use them to check your hand-computed timestamps.

Exam pointers:
  • Happened-before has three rules (same process, message, transitivity). Logical concurrency is neither ei → ej nor ej → ei.
  • Scalar clock rules: Rule 1 Ci := Ci + d; Rule 2 Ci := max(Ci, Cmsg), then Rule 1, then deliver. Be able to timestamp a small diagram.
  • Scalar time is consistent (e → f implies C(e) < C(f)) but not strongly consistent. The p1 fifth event (timestamp 5) versus p4 third event (timestamp 4) is the counterexample from the slides.
  • Vector comparison (≤, <, ||). Know that vector clocks are strongly consistent, and that the cost is message size that grows with n.

Lecture 4: Communication Primitives and MPI

Source: Lecture4.pdf, slides 1–33

Two primitives: Send and Receive

Most distributed systems give you two communication primitives, Send and Receive. The slides first point out a kernel detail. A message can arrive before the user process has called Receive, so the kernel has to hold the data until the process asks for it. On the send side, the usual assumption is that data is copied from the user buffer into a kernel buffer before it goes onto the network. The slides call this the buffered option.

Synchronous vs asynchronous

These two terms describe what must happen before the operation counts as done.

  • Synchronous: Send and the matching Receive follow a handshake. The sender knows the receiver is ready.
  • Asynchronous: Send returns control once the data has been copied from the user buffer to the kernel buffer. The receiver may not be ready yet.

Blocking vs non-blocking

These two terms describe when control returns to the calling process.

  • Blocking Send: control returns only after the operation's processing is complete.
  • Non-blocking Send/Receive: control returns immediately, before the operation has finished.
Synchronous vs blocking Synchronous is about the handshake (is the receiver ready?). Blocking is about whether the caller waits. The two are independent, so a send can be synchronous and non-blocking, or asynchronous and blocking. The slides list four combinations and point to the textbook for pictures.

The four combinations on slide 5 are: blocking synchronous send with blocking receive; non-blocking synchronous send with non-blocking receive; blocking asynchronous send; and non-blocking asynchronous send. Slides 6 to 9 draw a timeline for each one. Each timeline shows the process, its user buffer, and the kernel. The send starts at S, and S_C marks its completion. The receive is R, and R_C marks its completion.

In the first picture, the sender's S_C only returns after a return arrow comes back from the receiver's side. That is the handshake. The receiver's R_C is also drawn at the end of the transfer. Both calls block in this case.

In the second picture both calls return at once. The labels W and P are not explained on the slide. My reading (background) is that W is waiting time and P is a check on whether the operation has finished. The synchronous handshake is still there, because the completion S_C is only reached after the data reaches the receiver.

The asynchronous cases have no handshake. The send is complete once the data is in the kernel. The difference between blocking and non-blocking is whether the call returns immediately or after the copy.

Exam pointers:
  • Know the four combinations on slide 5 and what "control returns" means for each.
  • Synchronous means a handshake with the receiver. Asynchronous means the send returns after the copy to the kernel buffer.
  • In basic MPI, MPI_Send returns when the buffer can be reused. The message may not have been received yet.

Why distributed programming is hard

Slides 10 to 12 recall what a distributed system is: a collection of autonomous computers that communicate over a network. The typical features are: no common physical clock (clocks drift); no shared memory, so communication is by messages; geographical separation, which allows wide-area work such as SETI; autonomy, meaning loosely coupled processors that still cooperate; and heterogeneity, meaning the processors need not be alike.

The slides then split the difficulty into two kinds.

  • Inherent complexity comes from the problem itself: latency (computers can be far apart), reliability (recovering from failures), partitioning (failures can split the system), ordering (there is no global clock, so ordering events is hard), and security.
  • Accidental complexity comes from the tools: low-level APIs with too little abstraction, poor debugging tools for finding faults, the choice of algorithmic decomposition, and continuous re-invention as key components change.

The point of frameworks such as MPI is to reduce the accidental part, so the programmer can focus on the inherent part.

MPI: a message-passing library

Slide 14 defines MPI (Message Passing Interface). It is a library specification for an extended message-passing model. It is not a language, not a compiler, and not one particular implementation. It targets parallel computers, clusters and heterogeneous networks, and it is full-featured. It is meant for end users, library writers and tool developers. Slide 15 lists reference books by Gropp, Lusk and Skjellum; Snir et al.; Foster; and Pacheco, plus the MPI Forum standard.

Slides 18 and 19 introduce the basic concepts.

  • Processes can be organised into groups.
  • Each message is sent in a context and must be received in the same context.
  • A group and a context together form a communicator.
  • A process is identified by its rank within the group of a communicator.
  • MPI_COMM_WORLD is the default communicator. Its group holds all the initial processes.

Slides 16 and 17 show a minimal program that calls MPI_Init and MPI_Finalize, followed by a "Better Hello" version that calls MPI_Comm_rank and MPI_Comm_size on MPI_COMM_WORLD and prints "I am rank of size".

Basic blocking send and receive

MPI_SEND(start, count, datatype, dest, tag, comm). The buffer is given by start, count and datatype. The target is dest, a rank in the communicator comm. When the call returns, the data has been handed to the system and the buffer can be reused. The slides stress that the message may not have been received yet.

MPI_RECV(start, count, datatype, source, tag, comm, status). It waits until a message matching the source and tag arrives, and then the buffer can be used. The source can be MPI_ANY_SOURCE. Receiving fewer than count items is fine, but receiving more is an error. The status object is filled in by the call. It holds the sender (MPI_SOURCE) and the tag (MPI_TAG), and MPI_Get_count gives the number of items received. Slide 21 shows this in C and in Fortran.

Slide 22 says that many parallel programs need only six functions: MPI_INIT, MPI_FINALIZE, MPI_COMM_SIZE, MPI_COMM_RANK, MPI_SEND and MPI_RECV. Only the last two are non-trivial. Point-to-point communication is not the only option, though.

Collective operations

Collectives are called by all processes in a communicator. Slide 23 gives two examples. MPI_BCAST sends data from one root to all others. MPI_REDUCE combines data from all processes and returns the result to one process. The slide says that many numerical algorithms can replace SEND/RECEIVE with BCAST/REDUCE and gain both simplicity and speed.

Slide 28 groups the collectives into three kinds: synchronisation (MPI_BARRIER), data movement (MPI_GATHER and MPI_SCATTER, one-to-all, all-to-one and all-to-all), and computation (MPI_REDUCE and MPI_SCAN).

  • MPI_BARRIER(group): every process in the group blocks until all have called it. Barriers can waste time, so the slides say to use them only where a hard sync point is needed.
  • MPI_SCATTER(sData, sCount, sType, rData, rCount, rType, root, comm): sCount items go to each process. The first block goes to one rank, the next block to the next rank, and so on. (The slide says "rank 1" for the first block. In MPI, ranks count from 0, so this is probably loose wording. Background.)
  • MPI_GATHER: the inverse of scatter. Data from every process goes to the root, ordered by rank. rCount is the count from each process, not the total. Non-root processes can pass NULL as rData.
  • MPI_SCAN(sendbuf, recvbuf, count, datatype, op, comm): a prefix reduction. Each process gets the result over ranks 0 up to and including its own. MPI_REDUCE gives one final result to the root only, while MPI_SCAN keeps a running result at every process.

Worked example: computing pi

Slides 24 to 26 give a C program that estimates pi using the midpoint rule on the integral of 4/(1+x²) over [0,1].

  1. Rank 0 reads n (the number of intervals). The loop runs until n is 0. MPI_Bcast sends n to everyone.
  2. The interval width is h = 1/n. Each process handles the midpoints x = h(i - 0.5). Process myid starts at i = myid+1 and steps by numprocs, so the work is split round-robin.
  3. Each process adds up 4/(1+x²) into sum and computes mypi = h * sum.
  4. MPI_Reduce with MPI_SUM adds all the mypi values into pi at rank 0, which prints the result and the error.

This program uses only Init, Finalize, Size, Rank, Bcast and Reduce. Slide 27 asks why the other functions are needed. The answer is in the "other features" slides: collectives and the rest of the API.

Collectives at a glance

Slide 33 shows four processes with starting values 4, 3, 1, 2. The table reads as follows.

  • Broadcast from P1: all four end up with 4.
  • Gather to P1: P1 gets [4,3,1,2]. The others get nothing.
  • AllGather: every process gets [4,3,1,2].
  • AllToAll: the slide shows every process with [4,3,1,2]. With one item per process, a standard all-to-all transposes the data, so check this row against the textbook before you rely on it. (Background.)
  • Scan with SUM: prefix sums 4, 7, 8, 10.
  • Reduce with MAX to root P4: P4 gets 4.
Exam pointers:
  • Scatter sends consecutive blocks by rank. Gather collects in rank order. Scan is an inclusive prefix reduction.
  • Know what the pi program does and which collectives it uses (Bcast and Reduce).
  • Be ready to trace a collective with a small example such as the 4, 3, 1, 2 table.

Lecture 5: Message Delivery Models and Global Snapshots

Source: Lecture5.pdf, slides 1–41

Message delivery models

Before any algorithm, the lecture fixes how a channel may deliver messages. There are three models, from weakest to strongest.

  • Arbitrary (non-FIFO): a message can be reordered in transit.
  • FIFO: messages on a channel are not reordered.
  • Causal: slightly stronger than FIFO. Messages with the same destination are not reordered in the causal sense. In symbols, for any two messages m_ij and m_kj going to j: if send(m_ij) → send(m_kj) then recv(m_ij) → recv(m_kj).

The slides order them as Causal, then FIFO, then Arbitrary, meaning each one allows fewer orderings than the one after it. (The symbol between them is lost in the text extraction, so check the original slide.) The slides point to a separate paper on causal-order delivery for how causal order can be enforced.

Global state

The local state of process P_i is its registers, stack, and memory. The state of a channel is the set of messages in transit on it. The global state is the collection of all local states and channel states. Events change the local states.

Notation: LS_i^x is the local state of P_i after event e_i^x and before e_i^(x+1). LS_i^0 is the initial state. Because of how this is defined, LS_i^x accounts for every event up to and including e_i^x.

The state of channel C_ij, written SC^(x,y)_ij, is the set of messages that P_i had sent by LS_i^x but P_j had not yet received by LS_j^y:

SC^(x,y)_ij = { m_ij | send(m_ij) ∈ LS_i^x and recv(m_ij) ∉ LS_j^y }

A global state GS is the union of all the LS_i and SC_ij. It is consistent if every message recorded as received is also recorded as sent. Slide 11 asks you to write this as a formula. The answer is: for every message m, recv(m) ∈ GS implies send(m) ∈ GS.

Consistent global state A global state where no message is recorded as received without its send also being recorded. A state in which a receive appears without its send is not a real state the system could have been in.

Slide 13 gives three candidate states for the execution in the figure. Here is my check, using the event labels in the figure (the slides do not give the answer).

  1. {LS^1_1, LS^3_2, LS^3_3, LS^2_4}: P_2's state includes e_2^2, which is the receipt of m_12. But P_1's state is recorded at e_1^1, before the send e_1^2. This state is inconsistent.
  2. {LS^2_1, LS^4_2, LS^4_3, LS^2_4}: every recorded receive has its send recorded. m_21 is sent and not yet received at P_1, so it is in the channel state. This state is consistent.
  3. {LS^2_1, LS^1_2, SC^12_12, LS^3_3, LS^2_4}: m_12 is sent (in LS^2_1) and not yet received (P_2's state is before e_2^2), so it lives in the channel state. This state is consistent.

Why naive snapshots fail

Slides 14 to 18 use a banking example. Accounts A (at site S1) and B (at site S2) transfer money, with channel C_12 carrying a Rs 150 transfer from A to B, and channel C_21 carrying a Rs 100 transfer from B to A.

Slide 16 asks what total money the system holds if A is recorded at t0 and B and both channels are recorded at t2. The answer on the slide is that there is an extra Rs 150, and it warns that a checkpoint built from this state is wrong.

Adding up the recorded values gives 1000 (A) + 1400 (B) + 150 (C12) + 100 (C21) = 2650. The real total is 2500, so the snapshot is off by 150. The reason is that A was recorded before it sent the 150, so the snapshot does not record that send. But the channel C12 still records the 150 as being in transit. The snapshot therefore contains an effect (the message in the channel) without its cause (the send). This is exactly what the consistency rules forbid.

Consistency conditions C1 and C2

Slides 19 to 21 turn the example into rules. The state of channel C_ij is the messages sent by P_i before its record and not received by P_j before its record. A global state is consistent when it satisfies both of these:

  • C1, conservation of messages. If a message m_ij was sent as recorded in LS_i, then exactly one of these holds: m_ij is in the channel state SC_ij, or m_ij was received as recorded in LS_j. (The slide uses an exclusive-OR here.)
  • C2, every effect has a cause. If a message's send is not recorded in LS_i, then the message is not in SC_ij and it is not recorded as received in LS_j.

Two issues make snapshots hard (slides 22 and 23).

  • Issue 1: deciding which messages belong in the snapshot. Messages sent before a process records its state must be recorded (C1). Messages sent after must not be (C2).
  • Issue 2: deciding when each process records its state. A process P_j must record its state before it processes a message m_ij that P_i sent after P_i recorded its own state.

The algorithms below handle these two issues in different ways, depending on what the channels guarantee. The slides go in order: causal, then FIFO, then arbitrary.

Snapshots with causal channels

The Acharya–Badrinath and Alagar–Venkatesan algorithms both assume causal delivery. They record each process's state the same way:

  1. An initiator broadcasts a token to every process, including itself.
  2. When P_i receives its copy of the token, it records LS_i and sends the record to the initiator.
  3. The algorithm ends when the initiator has received the record from every process.

Why this works (slides 27 to 29): for any two processes, if the send of m_ij is not recorded in LS_i, then the receive of m_ij is not recorded in LS_j. Suppose rec(token_i) happens before send(m_ij). Then send(token_j) also happens before send(m_ij). Because of causal delivery, token_j is received at P_j before m_ij is. So P_j has recorded its state before it gets m_ij. The figure on slide 28 shows this with the token going out from the initiator to P_i and P_j.

Acharya–Badrinath. Each process P_i keeps two arrays of counters, SENT_i[1..N] and RECD_i[1..N]. SENT_i[j] counts the messages P_i has sent to P_j, and RECD_i[j] counts the messages P_i has received from P_j. When P_i records LS_i on the token, it includes both arrays in its state. When the algorithm finishes, the initiator works out each channel state. The channel from P_i to P_j holds the messages with sequence numbers RECD_j[i] + 1 up to SENT_i[j].

Complexity (slide 32). Recording and assembling the snapshot takes 2n messages and 2 time units, where one time unit is one message delivery. If the message contents of the channels are also needed, that adds another 2n messages and 2 time units.

Chandy–Lamport for FIFO channels

This algorithm uses a marker, a control message whose job is to separate messages on a FIFO channel into those inside the snapshot and those outside it. After a process records its state, it sends a marker on each outgoing channel before it sends any more messages on that channel. A process must record its state no later than when it receives a marker on any incoming channel.

Marker Sending Rule (for process i) (1) Record your local state. (2) On each outgoing channel where no marker has been sent yet, send a marker before any more messages on that channel.
Marker Receiving Rule (for process j) On receiving a marker on channel C: if j has not yet recorded its state, record the state of C as the empty set and run the Marker Sending Rule. If j has already recorded its state, record the state of C as the messages received on C after j recorded its state and before the marker arrived on C.

The algorithm can be started by any process, which runs the Marker Sending Rule. It finishes when every process has received a marker on all of its incoming channels. Then each local snapshot has been passed to every other process, so every process can work out the global state.

Why it is correct (slide 39): FIFO order means no message sent after the marker on a channel is recorded in that channel's state, so C2 holds. A message that arrives on C before the marker is either included in the receiver's state (if it has not yet recorded) or in the channel state (if it has), so C1 holds.

Complexity (slide 40). Recording takes O(e) messages and O(d) time, where e is the number of edges and d is the diameter of the network.

Slides 35 and 36 show an example run on an eight-process network. In the figures, the blue nodes are processes that have recorded their state. The red squares look like messages or markers still in transit. The slides have no legend, so this reading is mine.

Non-FIFO channels

Slide 41 says that a marker cannot separate messages in a non-FIFO system, because a message sent before the marker can arrive after it. The fix is either some form of inhibition (delaying some messages) or piggybacking control information on the normal messages. The reading exercise points to the Lin and Yang algorithm and to Mattern's algorithm, both in Kshemkalyani and Singhal. The slides do not cover them, so know only the general idea.

Exam pointers:
  • A global state is consistent if no receive is recorded without its send (C1 and C2). Be able to check a small example, as in slide 13.
  • Know why the naive bank snapshot gives 2650 instead of 2500: the 150 is in C12, but its send was after A's record.
  • Chandy–Lamport: marker sending and receiving rules, and why FIFO makes them correct. Complexity is O(e) messages and O(d) time.
  • Acharya–Badrinath: the SENT and RECD arrays, the channel state formula RECD_j[i]+1 to SENT_i[j], and the cost of 2n messages and 2 time units.

Lecture 6: MapReduce

Source: LectureMapReduce.pdf, slides 1–41

Why a programming model is needed

Slides 3 to 6 explain why big clusters are awkward. Commodity machines are cheap and easy to buy in bulk, but they have low disk bandwidth and high network latency, and their CPUs are roughly comparable to one another. They are also less reliable: they are mass-produced from cheaper materials and have a lifetime of about 3 years. So two questions follow. How do you use many modest machines well? How do applications cope with failures and still stay available?

Slide 6 adds the programming side. Distributed programs have to divide a job into tasks, track dependencies between tasks (control and data), coordinate and synchronise them, pass information between them, and avoid race conditions and deadlocks. Good abstractions hide this, in the same way that C++ hides assembly and Matlab hides C++.

Slides 7 to 13 repeat the characteristics of distributed systems and the inherent and accidental complexity from Lecture 4. Read them as background: no shared memory, no common clock, autonomy, heterogeneity, and so on.

What MapReduce is

MapReduce is a distributed, data-parallel programming model from Google, introduced close to 20 years ago. It works best with a distributed file system, the Google File System (GFS). Hadoop is the open-source Apache framework that runs the MapReduce model, and HDFS is its open-source version of the GFS design. Amazon's PaaS is another implementation. Slide 15 quotes Dean and Ghemawat (OSDI 2004): a simple and powerful interface that automates parallelisation and distribution of large computations, with an implementation that performs well on large clusters of commodity PCs. (The slide spells the second author "Ghermawat". The correct spelling is Ghemawat. Background.)

Slide 16 lists what MapReduce gives you: a clean abstraction, automatic parallelisation and distribution, fault tolerance, a batch processing system, and status and monitoring tools.

MapReduce versus RDBMS

Slides 17 to 20 explain when MapReduce is the right tool.

  • Seek time. Relational databases suffer from large seek times. MapReduce assumes that almost the whole dataset is relevant to each query, so it reads everything in a batch. It is a batch query processor, good for ad hoc analysis of the whole dataset.
  • Write once, read many. MapReduce suits data that is written once and read many times. A relational database suits data that is updated all the time, and it is good at point queries and updates through indexes.
  • Structure. MapReduce works well on unstructured and semi-structured data.
  • Normalisation. Normalised tables cost a non-local read every time a record is joined. MapReduce assumes high-speed streaming reads and writes. A web server log is not normalised (the client hostname is repeated in every line), so it is well suited to MapReduce.
  • Convergence. The two are getting closer. Some databases borrow MapReduce ideas (the slides name Aster Data and Greenplum), and higher-level tools such as Pig and Hive make MapReduce approachable to database programmers.

The programming model

Slide 21 says that the model looks restrictive, but mappers and reducers run with very little coordination. It is used for image analysis, graph problems and machine learning. It cannot solve every problem, but it is a general data-processing tool.

Slide 22 gives the signatures. The user writes:

  • map(k_i, v_i) → List<k_m, v_m>: called on every input item. It emits a series of intermediate key/value pairs.
  • All values with the same key are then grouped together.
  • reduce(k_m, List<v_m>) → List<k_r, v_r>: called once for each unique key and all of its values. It emits values that go to the output.

Word count

Slide 23 is the standard example. Input lines are "How now brown cow", "How does it work", and so on. Each mapper emits <word, 1> for every word. Shuffle groups all the 1s for each word. Each reducer sums them. The output is brown 1, cow 1, does 1, how 2, it 1, now 2, work 1. The slide writes the words in lower case, so the mapper probably lowercases its input (this is an inference from the output).

Slides 24 and 25 cover the map step in detail. The framework passes each input record to map as a key/value pair, such as (line number, line text), and map emits zero or more intermediate pairs. Two examples are given.

  • Upper-case mapper: map(k, v) emits (k.toUpper(), v.toUpper()). So ("foo","bar") gives ("FOO","BAR").
  • Filter mapper: map(k, v) emits (k, v) only if v is prime. So ("foo", 7) is kept and ("test", 10) emits nothing.

Slide 26 covers the reduce step. All intermediate values for one output key are combined into a list. Reduce combines them into one or more final values for that key, usually exactly one. Each reducer writes one output file.

Slide 27 walks through the word count in detail. Each mapper emits <word, 1>. After the shuffle, the reducer for "how" gets the list (1, 1), and its code is: sum = sum + value over the list, then emit(key, sum). So "how" gives 2 and "now" gives 2.

Tasks, shuffle and sort

Slide 28 separates tasks from methods. The user sets the number of mapper and reducer tasks. Each task can call the map or reduce method many times, one after another. Mapper and reducer tasks may run on different machines. The framework decides where they run and which keys go to which task, though the user can influence this.

Slide 29 describes shuffle and sort, which the slides call the magic of the framework. Shuffle does a group-by on the keys from all mappers, much like SQL GROUP BY. Within each reducer the keys are sorted. There is no ordering across reducers, and the order of values for a key is not guaranteed.

Combiners and partitioners

Slides 31 to 33 cover two optional optimisations.

  • Combiner. A "mini-reduce" that runs on the map machine, on that mapper's local output only. Its output goes to the shuffle, which saves network bandwidth. Its input and output types are the same as the map output, so Combine(k', v'[]) gives (k', v').
  • Partitioner. Decides which reducer each intermediate key goes to, and so affects the load on each reducer. The default is hash partitioning: HashPartitioner(key, nParts) returns a partition number in [0, nParts). It balances the number of keys per reducer, assuming keys are uniformly distributed. It may not balance the number of values a reducer has to process.

Slide 33 notes that the combine and partition steps can be swapped depending on the implementation, and that both are powerful, so use them carefully.

Slide 34 gives a histogram example. Each mapper emits (floor(v / bucketWidth), 1), with bucketWidth = 4. Each reducer, one per bucket ID, sums the 1s and emits (bucket, frequency). The slide shows 28 items moving from mappers to reducers in the shuffle. (The picture on that slide is not in the extracted images.)

Slide 35 explains the benefit of the combiner. Suppose n items are emitted from m mappers. Without a combiner, n items are written to disk, sent over the network, and read back. With a combiner, about m items are. Since m is much smaller than n, I/O and network cost drop. Shuffle is less affected if there are more mappers than reducers, because the mappers do part of the grouping and sorting. The sort on each reducer depends on the number of distinct keys, and the combiner does not change that.

The recap and what MapReduce hides

Slide 36 summarises it. The programmer must specify map (k, v) → <k', v'>* and reduce (k', v'[]) → <k'', v''>*. All values with the same key are reduced together. Optionally, the programmer can also specify partition(k', number of partitions), which is often a hash such as hash(k') mod n, and combine(k', v'), which acts as a mini-reducer in memory after the map phase to cut network traffic. The execution framework handles everything else.

Slide 37 says what MapReduce solves: scalable data analytics, where the work is computation over sets of keys and values, not limited by disk reads and writes. The cost is that the data is not normalised, so a record may need to be read from several places.

Slide 38 lists what the framework takes care of: scheduling (assigning workers to map and reduce tasks), data distribution (moving the process to the data), synchronisation (gathering, sorting and shuffling intermediate data), and errors and faults (detecting failed workers and restarting them). The programmer has limited control. All algorithms must be written in terms of map, reduce, combine and partition. You do not know where mappers and reducers run, when they begin or end, which input a mapper has, or which intermediate key a reducer has.

Failures and YARN

Slide 39 covers failures. The jobtracker and tasktrackers handle them. A tasktracker notices failed tasks through runtime exceptions, sudden exits of the task code, and hangs, which show up as timeouts. If the jobtracker itself fails, MapReduce has no way to save and restore the computation.

Slide 40 introduces YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator). It was built because MapReduce's scalability becomes a concern once the cluster reaches about 104 nodes or more. YARN splits the jobtracker's job in two: a resource manager that manages cluster resources, and an application master that manages each application's lifecycle. It saves the jobtracker's state more carefully on failure. YARN is more general than MapReduce, which is now just one kind of YARN application.

Slide 41 gives the reading: Tom White's Hadoop: The Definitive Guide, chapters 1, 2, 3 and 6. Homework 3 covers MapReduce and gRPC.

Exam pointers:
  • Know the map and reduce signatures, and trace word count by hand, including the shuffle groups.
  • A combiner is a local mini-reduce that cuts shuffle traffic. It must have the same input and output types as map. A partitioner chooses the reducer for each key, and the default is hash partitioning.
  • Know when to use MapReduce rather than an RDBMS: batch, whole-dataset, write-once data, and logs.
  • Know what the framework handles (scheduling, locality, shuffle, faults) and what the programmer controls. Know why YARN was introduced.

gRPC and Other Distributed Programming Frameworks

Source: LecturegRPC.pdf, slides 1–11

The landscape of frameworks

Slide 1 lists several frameworks that came before or after MPI: Remote Procedure Call (RPC), CORBA, RMI (Remote Method Invocation), gRPC, and Erlang. There are also lower-level mechanisms such as sockets. The frameworks share some ideas and differ in others.

Slide 2 gives the verdict. CORBA and RPC are not very popular today. RMI and sockets are too low-level. gRPC is widely used, and the slides go into it in detail.

RPC and gRPC

RPC is an abstraction that lets a client program make a function call that actually runs on a remote server. The call looks local to the programmer. Underneath, RPC uses a transport such as TCP or UDP to send the call, contact the server to run it, and return the result to the client. The idea came from Sun. Later systems such as Java RMI and CORBA added an object-oriented interface on top of RPC.

Google introduced gRPC in 2015. It was built on Google's in-house RPC framework, Stubby, which let microservices inside Google's datacenters talk to each other. gRPC is open source, general purpose and cross-platform.

RPC (Remote Procedure Call) A way to call a function on another machine as if it were a local function. The network details (marshalling, transport, errors) are hidden from the caller.

A running example: the academic office

Slide 5 sets up a client-server system. The server is a university academic office that answers questions about courses: the list of courses, the schedule, the credits, the prerequisites, and so on. Clients ask for a list of courses, the schedule of a set of courses, or prerequisites.

To build the server, you first define the functions in an Interface Definition Language (IDL). The slide's example has three remote functions, each taking a course code as a String:

  • rpc getCourseName(String courseCode)
  • rpc getCourseSyllabus(String courseCode)
  • rpc getCourseSeatsAvailable(String courseCode)

The .proto file

In gRPC the IDL is written in a .proto file. Slides 7 and 8 show one. It has the following parts.

  • syntax: the protocol buffer version. Slide 7 prints "proto4", which looks like a typo. The image on slide 8 shows "proto3", the real version. (Background: proto3 is the current version of the language.)
  • option java_package and package: naming for the generated code.
  • service: a set of rpc methods. Each one names its request message and its reply message.
  • message: typed fields. Each field has a type, a name, and a number, such as string name = 1;. The number identifies the field on the wire.

The example defines a service CourseName with one method, rpc SayHello(HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply). The request holds a string name, and the reply holds a string message. The slide's package and service names say CourseInfo and CourseName, while the method is SayHello. This is a greeting example, not the academic office. The slide does not say that it is the same system.

The slides do not show the code generation step. (Background: the gRPC tooling generates client and server stub code from the .proto file. The server implements the methods, and the client calls them through a stub that handles marshalling and networking.)

The client

Slide 9 shows a Java client method called greet(String name). It does four things. It logs that it will try to greet the name. It builds a HelloRequest with HelloRequest.newBuilder().setName(name).build(). It calls blockingStub.sayHello(request), which is the synchronous call through the generated stub. If the call throws a StatusRuntimeException, it logs a warning and returns. Otherwise it logs the greeting from response.getMessage().

This is the blocking style of call: the client waits for the reply. The error handling uses an exception, which is a status error, not a normal return value.

Other features

Slide 10 covers streaming. Ordinary gRPC is one request and one reply. With streaming, the server can send several replies to one request, or the client can send several requests to one server call. The messages need not all be sent at once. The server can send them as it finds more matching data. The server ends a stream by sending its status and trailing metadata.

Slide 11 lists four more features.

  • Authentication with TLS (Transport Layer Security) secures the connection.
  • Interceptors are code that runs before each RPC call. (Background: they can also run after the call, which is what post-processing needs.) They are used for pre- and post-processing such as logging, metrics, and authentication, without changing each method.
  • Deadlines and timeouts, cancellations, and error handling are also supported.
Exam pointers:
  • Know why RPC hides the network, and why gRPC was built from Stubby.
  • Know the structure of a .proto file: service, rpc, message, field numbers. Be ready to write a simple service definition from the academic office example.
  • Know the four extra features: streaming, TLS, interceptors, and deadlines and cancellations.

Lecture 7: Mutual Exclusion

Source: Lecture7.pdf, slides 1–26

Why mutual exclusion matters

Mutual exclusion means that when a shared resource can be used by at most one process at a time, only one process gets to use it at any moment. The slides give printers, a network link and a database table as examples. Without this guarantee results can be wrong.

The slides use a bank account to show the problem. The balance is Rs. 500 and two processes each want to add Rs. 1000. Both read 500 and both compute 1500. If their updates are not exclusive, the account ends at Rs. 1500 when it should end at Rs. 2500. This is a lost-update bug, and the critical section (CS) is the code that reads and then writes the balance.

In an operating system this is solved with algorithms such as Peterson's algorithm and the bakery algorithm. The slides point out that these assume centralised control and atomic operations, which a distributed system does not have.

Why the distributed case is harder

A distributed system has no shared memory, so shared variables and semaphores cannot be used, and there is no single local kernel that can arbitrate. The only tool is message passing. Messages can have unpredictable delays, and no site knows the full current state of the system. The slides state that achieving mutual exclusion here is no easier than in a centralised setting, yet several algorithms do exist. This lecture covers Lamport's algorithm.

Requirements of a mutual exclusion algorithm

  1. Safety: at any instant, at most one process is in the CS.
  2. Liveness: no deadlock and no starvation. Two or more sites must not wait forever for messages that never arrive.
  3. Fairness: every process gets a fair chance. In practice this means CS requests are served in the order they arrived, where "arrived" is judged by a logical clock.

Lamport's algorithm: setup

Lamport's algorithm uses logical scalar clocks and assumes FIFO delivery of messages. It also assumes a bidirectional channel between every pair of sites. Each site Si keeps a local queue, request_queuei, of CS requests ordered by timestamp. A request is identified by the pair (tsi, i), where tsi is the logical timestamp and i is the site id. Pairs are compared by timestamp first and (background) by site id to break ties.

The three message types

MessageSent whenWhat the receiver does
REQUEST(tsi, i)Si wants the CS. It is sent to all other sites.Puts the request in its own request_queue and returns a timestamped REPLY.
REPLYSent in response to a REQUEST.Tells the requester that this site has seen its request. The requester learns a later timestamp from this site.
RELEASESi leaves the CS.Removes Si's request from its queue. This may bring another site's request to the top.

Entering the critical section

Site Si enters the CS only when both of these hold:

  • ALL-OK: Si has received a message with a timestamp larger than (tsi, i) from every other site.
  • SELF-TOP: Si's own request is at the top of request_queuei.

ALL-OK checks that nobody has an earlier request that is still unanswered. SELF-TOP checks that no earlier request is still queued locally.

Leaving the critical section

On exit, Si removes its own request from the top of its queue and broadcasts a timestamped RELEASE. A receiver removes Si's request from its queue. Removing a request can bring the receiver's own request to the top, which lets it enter the CS.

Example run

The space-time diagram below shows three sites. A requests with timestamp (4, A) and B requests with (3, B), which is earlier. Both send REQUESTs, and the replies come back. B has the smaller timestamp, so B enters the CS first. When B releases, A's request reaches the top of the queues and A enters.

The slides note that the queues are like a shared priority queue, but they are not always identical. Message delays mean each site can have a different view for a while.

Proof that the algorithm is safe

The proof is by contradiction. Suppose Si and Sj are both in the CS at instant t. Then both must satisfy ALL-OK and SELF-TOP at t. Both own requests are at the top of their queues. Without loss of generality, let (tsi, i) < (tsj, j). The slides argue that Si's request must then be in request_queuej while Sj is in the CS. That puts a smaller request ahead of Sj's own request, so Sj's request cannot be at the top. This contradicts SELF-TOP. The slides leave the step "why is Si's request in queuej?" as a question. (background) The reason: Sj must have received Si's REQUEST before it could satisfy ALL-OK, and a request leaves a queue only on a RELEASE, which Si has not yet sent.

Proof that the algorithm is fair

Again by contradiction. Suppose Si's request has a smaller timestamp than Sj's, yet Sj enters the CS first. For Sj to enter, its own request must be at the top of its queue and it must have a message with a larger timestamp from every site. But the queue is ordered by timestamp, so Si's smaller request must sit ahead of Sj's in request_queuej. That is a contradiction, so requests are served in timestamp order.

Message cost

Lamport's algorithm uses 3(N − 1) messages per CS grant. (background) That is N − 1 REQUESTs, N − 1 REPLYs and N − 1 RELEASEs, one each to every other site. Some optimisations reduce this to 2(N − 1) in some cases. The slides do not say which cases, so treat that number as a pointer for further reading. The slides also suggest reading about the message count and the optimisations.

Exam pointers:
  • Know the three requirements (safety, liveness, fairness) and be able to say which one each part of the algorithm supports.
  • Be able to state ALL-OK and SELF-TOP precisely. Both must hold to enter the CS.
  • Know the message count, 3(N − 1) per CS, and that the optimisation gives 2(N − 1) only in some cases.
  • The safety proof is by contradiction. The step "why is Si's request in queuej?" is a common question.

Lecture 8: Ricart-Agrawala and Maekawa Mutual Exclusion

Source: Lecture8.pdf, slides 1–27

Ricart-Agrawala: the idea

Lamport's algorithm (Lecture 7) needs FIFO channels. Ricart-Agrawala removes that assumption. It uses only two kinds of message: REQUEST, sent by a process to every other process to ask permission to enter the CS, and REPLY, sent to grant that permission. A process enters the CS only after it has collected a REPLY from every process it sent a REQUEST to.

Requests are ordered with Lamport-bakery-style priority numbers, so entry follows the order of those numbers. The numbers are maintained in a distributed way. No process knows the largest number issued so far, so each process keeps track of the largest priority number it has heard about. (background) A new request's number is one more than the largest it has seen, as in the bakery algorithm.

Per-process state: the Request_Deferred array

Each process pi keeps a Boolean array RDi with one entry per process. It starts with RDi[j] = 0 for all j. When pi defers pj's request, it sets RDi[j] = 1. Once it has sent the deferred REPLY to pj, it resets RDi[j] = 0. So RD is a record of who is waiting for a reply from this process.

Requesting the CS

  1. When Si wants the CS, it broadcasts a REQUEST carrying its priority number to all other sites.
  2. When Sj receives that REQUEST, it sends a REPLY right away if either:
    • (i) Sj is not interested: it is neither requesting nor in the CS, or
    • (ii) Sj is interested, and Si's request has a smaller priority number than Sj's own request.
    Otherwise the reply is deferred. Sj sets RDj[i] = 1.

Entering and leaving the CS

Si enters the CS after it has a REPLY from every site it sent a REQUEST to. On exit it sends every deferred REPLY. For each j with RDi[j] = 1, it sends a REPLY to Sj and resets RDi[j] = 0.

Worked example

The slides use six nodes (N3, N5, N6, N12, N32, N80), all able to send messages to each other. Each request is written as <timestamp, node>.

  1. Slide 8–9: N32 sends REQUEST <102, 32>. Everyone replies, so N32 is Held and can access the CS.
  2. Slide 10: While N32 holds the CS, N12 sends <115, 12> and N80 sends <110, 80>. Both are Wanted.
  3. Slide 12: N32 defers both requests and queues them.
  4. Slide 13–14: N80 compares the two requests. It defers <115, 12> because 115 is larger than its own 110. So N80 queues only <115, 12>.
  5. Slide 15: N32 leaves the CS and multicasts REPLYs to both waiting nodes. N80 now has every reply it needs and is Held. N12 is still Wanted and waits for N80's reply.

The next figure shows the state after N32 has collected its replies and entered the CS.

When N12 and N80 both request while N32 holds the CS, N32 cannot reply to either of them yet. It queues the two requests.

When N32 exits, it multicasts REPLYs to both queued requests at once. N80 now has every reply it needs and enters the CS. N12 is still waiting, because N80 deferred N12's request and will only reply after it leaves the CS.

Correctness and message cost

The safety proof is by contradiction. Suppose Si and Sj are both in the CS and Si's request has the higher priority. Si received Sj's request after making its own. For Sj to be in the CS, Si must have replied to Sj before Si exited. But Si defers requests that have lower priority than its own, so this cannot happen. Mutual exclusion holds.

Each CS entry costs (N − 1) REQUESTs and (N − 1) REPLYs, so 2(N − 1) messages in total. Compare Lamport's 3(N − 1) from Lecture 7. Ricart-Agrawala saves the RELEASE messages but needs no FIFO channels.

Maekawa's algorithm: the key idea

Both Lamport and Ricart-Agrawala need a reply from every process. Maekawa's idea is to ask only a subset of processes, called a quorum. This is the first solution in the slides with sublinear message complexity, O(√N) messages per CS. The price is that the quorums must be arranged so that two processes never both get permission from their full quorums at the same time.

The slides state two conditions for the quorum sets Si: (1) i ∈ Si, so every process is in its own quorum; and (2) for all i, j, Si ∩ Sj ≠ ∅, so every two quorums share at least one process. That shared process is the arbiter that stops two requesters from both winning.

Example quorums

With processes 0 to 6, the slides give:

S0 = {0, 1, 2}S1 = {1, 3, 5}S2 = {2, 4, 5}S3 = {0, 3, 4}
S4 = {1, 4, 6}S5 = {0, 5, 6}S6 = {2, 3, 6}

Each set contains its own index, and every pair of sets overlaps. For example S0 ∩ S1 = {1}, and S2 ∩ S3 = {4}.

Version 1: the basic protocol

  1. Send a timestamped REQUEST to every process in Si.
  2. When a process receives a REQUEST, it sends an ACK to the request with the lowest timestamp. It then locks itself to that process and keeps other requests waiting.
  3. Enter the CS when an ACK has come from every member of Si.
  4. To exit, send RELEASE to every member of Si.
  5. On RELEASE, the process unlocks and sends an ACK to the next waiting request with the lowest timestamp.

Safety: suppose i and j both try to enter. Because Si ∩ Sj ≠ ∅, some process k is in both. k never sends an ACK to both, so it arbitrates and at most one of them gets all its ACKs.

But it can deadlock. The slides give a run with 0, 1 and 2 all wanting the CS. From S0 = {0, 1, 2}, processes 0 and 2 ACK 0, but 1 ACKs 1. From S1 = {1, 3, 5}, processes 1 and 3 ACK 1, but 5 ACKs 2. From S2 = {2, 4, 5}, processes 4 and 5 ACK 2, but 2 ACKs 0. Now 0 waits for 1, 1 waits for 2, and 2 waits for 0. Each waits for a RELEASE that never comes.

Version 2: avoiding deadlock

If every process received REQUESTs in increasing timestamp order, the deadlock could be avoided. The slides call that assumption too strong. Version 2 fixes it with three extra messages: FAILED, INQUIRE and RELINQUISH.

  • A locked process sends the ACK and sets its lock as usual.
  • If the lock is set and a request with a larger timestamp arrives, it sends FAILED. That request has no chance.
  • If the incoming request has a lower timestamp, it sends INQUIRE to the locked process, asking whether that process is in the CS.
  • A process that receives INQUIRE and has at least one FAILED sends RELINQUISH. This gives the lock back.
  • The recipient of RELINQUISH resets its lock. (background) It then grants the lock to the next waiting request.

The point of FAILED and RELINQUISH is that a process holding ACKs it cannot use will give them back, which breaks the cycle of waits. The slides say the many other mutual exclusion algorithms are for further reading.

Exam pointers:
  • Ricart-Agrawala: know the reply rule (reply at once if not interested or if the requester has the smaller priority number, otherwise defer) and the RD array update. Be able to trace the N32/N12/N80 example.
  • Message counts: Ricart-Agrawala 2(N − 1), Lamport 3(N − 1), Maekawa O(√N).
  • Maekawa: state the two quorum conditions and check that a given set of quorums satisfies them.
  • Know the Version 1 deadlock example and why FAILED, INQUIRE and RELINQUISH fix it.

Lecture 9: File Systems and Distributed File Systems (NFS, AFS)

Source: Lecture9.pdf, slides 1–36

Logistics

The deadline for HW 2 was extended to 10 PM, Friday, 4 September 2026.

What a file system does

A file system gives programs access to files and controls who may use them. The UNIX file system is the classic design. It stores each file's metadata in an inode, which points to the file's data blocks using direct and indirect numbering. Access control uses owner, group and others, each with read, write and execute bits. Many later designs build on this. The slides refer to Maurice Bach's book on the design of the UNIX operating system for more detail.

The basic operations on a file are open, read, write, close and seek. The slide 4 figure splits them from directory operations.

Why distributed file systems are hard

The slides describe current trends: planet-scale applications such as Facebook and YouTube let many users create, share and access content at the same time. The content produced each day is in the petabyte range, and users and data are geographically spread out. The slides call data "the new oil", the source of analytics and revenue. To use it, a storage system must handle scalability, retrieval, network latency, concurrent access, availability, durability and consistency.

Design features

  • Durability: the ability to recover data after failures of the hardware underneath. Distributed file systems usually replicate data. Replication brings its own problems: creating, updating and maintaining replicas, and keeping them consistent.
  • Availability: the system must cope with errors from users and from the file system itself, and with delays and other network effects.
  • Availability vs durability: the slides pose this as a question without answering it. (background) Availability is whether the data can be reached when needed. Durability is whether the data survives failures at all. A system can be durable but briefly unavailable, or available but not durable.
  • Consistency model: many users create, read and update the same files, possibly at once, as in Dropbox or Google Docs. The system needs defined semantics for what happens to concurrent updates, and mechanisms to support them.
  • Scalability: capacity should grow seamlessly and transparently without losing performance.
  • Metadata: the namespace and its data structures are most of what a file system maintains. The choice of structure affects latency, scalability and throughput, and the memory system matters.
  • Application-specific concerns: the typical use case, typical file sizes (which sets block size) and which operation matters most for performance. Optimising for throughput may mean sacrificing other features.

The design space

Namespace. A flat namespace gives each file a unique identifier, and that identifier is used to find it. A hierarchical namespace uses pathnames.

How reads and writes are served. The options run from a fully client-server design, where the server does every step, to designs where the server hands work to the client, helps the client locate a file, or lets the client cache all or part of a file. Caching is fast but can create inconsistent views.

Consistency guarantees. The spectrum runs from "leave it to the clients" (no guarantees), to forbidding concurrent updates (which the slides call not very useful), to last write wins, where the writes are serialised and the last successful write is what the server keeps.

Application-specific designs. Combine many small objects into one file, as with photos on Facebook. Disallow in-place writes and create a new copy on each update. Support append rather than write, as with log files.

Faults. Provide several servers and replicate the data, with the associated challenges.

Early systems

NFS (Networked File System) came from Sun Microsystems, whose slogan was "The Network is the Computer". AFS (Andrew File System) came from CMU's Andrew project. Later systems include GFS (Google File System), HDFS (the open-source version of GFS), Colossus (the next version of GFS), and Haystack and Tectonic (used by Facebook). The slides say these share common ideas, which the lecture explores.

Goals

A file system normally aims for a consistent namespace and lets authorised users access their files. A distributed file system adds scalability (large user and file counts), fault tolerance (surviving client and server failures), concurrency (many users) and security (only authorised users). It is not possible to meet all of these all the time, so designers prioritise.

User-oriented vs workload-oriented design

A workload-oriented design measures the target workload and designs for it. A user-oriented design optimises for how users use files. The slides say that for NFS and AFS the typical user has these properties: most files are privately owned, there is little concurrent access, access is mostly sequential, and reads are more common than writes. GFS, by contrast, is aimed at big-program and big-data workloads.

Early option: RPC for every operation

The simplest design forwards every file system operation over RPC to the server. The server orders all accesses, performs them and returns the result. NFS v1 was built this way. The advantage is that it behaves exactly like a local file system. The costs are that latency to a remote server is much higher than to local memory, and the server is overloaded because every action needs it. The slides draw the moral: we need designs that avoid contacting the server for everything. Then the question is what we lose by doing so.

The better solution: caching

The answer is caching, but caching brings consistency risks. The slides quote David Wheeler: "All problems in computer science can be solved by adding a level of indirection; but this will usually cause other problems."

NFS caches file blocks and directory metadata in RAM at both the client and the server. When open, read, write and close can all be done locally there is no network traffic. The cost is that failures and cache consistency become big concerns. NFS trades some consistency for performance.

Problems with caching

  • Server crash: anything in memory but not on disk is lost. If the server keeps the file position in RAM, then seek(); (crash); read() returns bogus data.
  • Lost messages: if a client loses the acknowledgement of delete("foo"), it may retry. In the meantime another client may have created a new file with the same name, and the retry deletes that new file.
  • Client crash: updates still in the client cache can be lost.

Stateful vs stateless protocols

StatefulStateless
Server keepsClient-specific stateNo information on client accesses
RequestsShorter; faster to processMust name the file and offset each time
Crash recoveryServer state can be lostServer can crash and recover, since there is no state to lose (the caching slides show what a stateful server loses)
Open/closeNeeded to establish stateNot needed
Caching and lockingCache coherence possible (server knows who accesses what); file locking possibleFile locking not possible
ScaleUses server space for stateNo server space for state, so many clients can be supported

NFS: a stateless design with flush-on-close

The NFS solution to the caching problems is a stateless design. Each request carries the exact state it needs. read() becomes read(position), so the server never has to keep a seek position. Operations are made idempotent by giving each file and directory a unique ID. The slides' example: the client does not send delete("foo") but delete(1337f00f), where that ID is never reused. A retried delete then cannot hit a new file with the same name.

Consistency uses flush-on-close: when a file is closed, all modified blocks are sent to the server, and close() does not return until the bytes are safely stored.

Weak consistency in NFS

A writer and a reader can see different data, because a write may only be in the writer's cache until the file is closed. Two clients reading at the same time may get different results if one has old data cached. NFS allows the system to be inconsistent for a few seconds. The slides call this weak consistency, and say periodic checks limit the damage. NFS gives no guarantees at all about multiple writes.

Later NFS versions

  • NFS v3 added asynchronous writes. The server acknowledges the data but need not write it to stable storage before replying, and may wait to batch writes or never schedule them. It also added basic file locking through the Network Lock Manager, which makes the protocol stateful.
  • NFS v4 is stateful. It adds compound operations, which combine a sequence of operations into one remote call, locking as a first-class feature, and leases.

AFS in brief

AFS caches more aggressively. On open it prefetches the entire file, so later operations are local and fast. Its consistency is close-to-open only: all changes are flushed to the server on close.
