The slides say this suits user-centric workloads. AFS uses cache invalidation callbacks. A client registers that it holds a copy, and the server sends "Invalidate!" if the file changes. This trades server-side state for better consistency.

Summary

In both AFS and NFS the central server is a bottleneck, since reads and writes hit it at least once per file use. It is also a single point of failure, and making it fast and reliable needs expensive hardware. GFS addresses some of these concerns but is tailored to different users and workloads.

Exam pointers:
  • Stateful vs stateless: know the table and why the NFS design is stateless, including the idempotent delete example with unique file IDs.
  • NFS consistency is weak. It uses flush-on-close and gives no guarantees for multiple writes. Two readers can see different data.
  • AFS uses whole-file prefetch, close-to-open consistency and callbacks. Be able to say what server state the callbacks cost.
  • The central-server problems (bottleneck, single point of failure, cost) are the motivation for GFS.

Lecture 10: Google File System, Haystack and Other Object Stores

Source: Lecture10.pdf, slides 1–47

1. GFS: what it was built for

GFS (Google File System) was designed around the workload Google actually had, not around general-purpose POSIX use. The slides list the priorities: files are huge (multi-GB is common), most updates are appends, random writes are practically nonexistent, and many files are written once and then read sequentially. High bandwidth matters more than latency, and many clients write at the same time. The slides' example is several crawler workers all updating one index file.

The interface is deliberately not POSIX. The slides say you could not mount it. It supports only the popular file operations, with different semantics, and adds one new operation, record append. Google's frequent uses of append are merging results from many machines into one file (the Map/Reduce pattern), using a file as a producer-consumer queue, and logging user activity and site traffic. For appends the order of records does not matter, but atomicity and concurrency do. A traditional write operation is not given a clear guarantee; the semantics are "at least once, atomic record appends".

2. Architecture: one master, many chunkservers

A GFS cluster has a single master (replicated in later versions), many chunkservers, and many clients. Each file is cut into fixed-size chunks, which are analogous to filesystem blocks but far bigger. Each chunk gets a 64-bit globally unique handle, is stored on chunkservers, and is 3-way replicated across chunkservers.

Chunk A fixed-size piece of a file (64 MB in GFS), identified by a 64-bit handle and stored as an ordinary Linux file on several chunkservers.
Master A separate process that stores all metadata and monitors the chunkservers. Clients use it to find where data lives, but the bulk data does not flow through it.

The master holds the metadata: the file and chunk namespaces (a hierarchical namespace for files, a flat one for chunks), the file-to-chunk mappings, and the locations of each chunk's replicas. The master and the chunkservers exchange heartbeats. Through them the master learns whether a chunkserver is down, whether disks have failed, whether replicas are corrupted, and which chunks each server holds. The master then sends instructions back: delete a chunk, create a new chunk, or replicate a chunk and start serving it (chunk migration). Migration is useful for balancing disk usage and traffic, and for recovery after failures.

3. Chunk size: the trade-off

A 64 MB chunk is large compared with a normal filesystem block (512 B to 8 KB). The advantages claimed on the slides: there is less metadata per file, so it fits in the master's memory; it suits big-data work like search; and it sustains large bandwidth while cutting network overhead, since one client talks to one chunk for a long stretch. The disadvantage is internal fragmentation if small files turn out to be more common than expected.

4. Chunk locations are not persistent

The master does not store chunk locations on disk. It keeps them only in memory and rebuilds them by polling the chunkservers at startup. This means the master can restart and recover chunk locations from the chunkservers, and it keeps persistent state small, which helps simplicity and scalability. The cost is that restarting the master takes a long time. The file namespace, by contrast, is kept on durable storage in the master. The slides ask why GFS was designed this way; the answer they hint at is "design for failures, simplicity, scalability: the less persistent state the master keeps, the better".

5. Reads

The read path (figures on slides 12 and 13) shows how the master is kept out of the data path:

  1. The application gives the GFS client a file name and byte range.
  2. The client converts this to (file name, chunk index) and sends it to the master.
  3. The master replies with the chunk handle and the replica locations. The client caches this metadata.
  4. The client sends (chunk handle, byte range) to one of the chunkservers.
  5. The chunkserver returns the data.
  6. The client hands the data to the application.

Because the client caches metadata and then reads directly from chunkservers, the master handles only small metadata lookups. The slides say this "alleviates the single-master bottleneck".

6. Writes, leases and primaries

There are two update operations: Write (to a specific offset in a file) and RecordAppend. For replicas to stay identical, every replica must apply updates to a chunk in the same order. GFS achieves this by designating one replica per chunk as the primary; the others are secondaries. The primary decides the update order and the secondaries follow it.

It is critical that at any time there is at most one primary per chunk. Otherwise two primaries could order concurrent writes differently. GFS enforces this with leases. The master picks a chunkserver and grants it a lease for a chunk. The chunkserver holds the lease for a period T and acts as primary during that period. It can keep refreshing the lease. If it cannot refresh it from the master, it stops being primary. If the master stops hearing from the primary, it grants the lease to another chunkserver. So for each chunk there is at most one primary, although different chunks can have different primaries.

A write proceeds as follows (figures on slides 16 to 19):

  1. The application passes (file name, data) to the client.
  2. The client asks the master for the chunk index.
  3. The master returns the chunk handle and the primary and secondary replica locations.
  4. The client pushes the data to all replicas, where it is held in a buffer. The data is not yet applied.
  5. The client sends the write command to the primary.
  6. The primary assigns a serial order to the write and applies it.
  7. The primary forwards the write command, in the same serial order, to the secondaries, which apply it.
  8. The secondaries reply to the primary.
  9. The primary replies to the client.

The slide 20 summary: the primary enforces one update order across all replicas for concurrent writes, and it waits until the write finishes at the other replicas before it replies. So the replicas are identical. However, a file region can end up with mingled fragments from different clients, because writes to different chunks may be ordered differently by different primaries. Writes are therefore consistent, but the effect of concurrent writes is undefined.

A subtle point. Slide 21 says the client does not send the data to every replica. It sends the data to one replica, and the replicas forward it along a chain, to maximise bandwidth and throughput. The step-4 figure on slide 17 shows the client pushing to each replica directly. Read the chain as the actual design and the figure as a simplified picture of the buffer-push step.

7. Record append

In a record append the client specifies only the data, not the file offset. The primary chooses the offset. This gives meaningful semantics, namely that the record is appended at least once, atomically. Because the file system is not constrained about where data is placed, it can get atomicity without sacrificing concurrency: many clients can append to one file at once and each record lands whole.

The steps (slide 23):

  1. The application originates a record append request.
  2. The GFS client translates it and sends it to the master.
  3. The master replies with the chunk handle and the primary and secondary locations.
  4. The client pushes the data to all locations.
  5. The primary checks whether the record fits in the chunk.
  6. If it does not fit, the primary pads the chunk, tells the secondaries to do the same, and reports the failure. The client then retries the append on the next chunk. The primary of the next chunk may be a different server, so the client must ask the master again.
  7. If it fits, the primary appends the record at some offset, tells the secondaries to do the same at that offset, waits for their responses, and sends the final response to the client.

GFS may insert padding between record appends, so applications should prefer record append to plain writes. Applications need to cope with padding and duplicates, for example with checksums and unique IDs in each record.

Slide 25 summarises GFS: it is optimised for large files and sequential appends; it uses a large chunk size, a file system API tailored to that workload, and a single master to simplify coordination. It keeps the master out of large data transfers. It runs on commodity hardware, unlike AFS or NFS, which needed fairly hefty servers at scale.

8. Haystack: Facebook's photo object store

Facebook stores audio, video and photos, mostly shared among friends. Content has to be delivered quickly at planet scale. A CDN is one option, but CDNs are geared towards popular data and cannot handle the long tail of rarely accessed content. Haystack (Beaver et al., OSDI 2010) is built for this. Three observations drive the design. Keeping as much metadata in memory as possible gives higher throughput. Minimising metadata per object is therefore important. And most photos are not shared: the owner is the only one who can update them, and everyone else only reads.

Haystack has three components:

  • Haystack Store: the persistent storage for photos, holding the filesystem-level metadata.
  • Haystack Directory: maps logical volumes to physical volumes and keeps application metadata.
  • Haystack Cache: an internal CDN that serves requests for hot photos.

9. The Store: volumes, needles and an in-memory index

A Store machine stores physical volumes. Each physical volume is one large file of hundreds of GB, holding millions of photos. The file starts with one superblock, followed by a sequence of needles. Each needle is one photo, with a header (cookie, key, flags, size), the data, a checksum and padding. Physical volumes are grouped into logical volumes, and a photo is replicated on a logical volume by writing it to every physical volume in that group.

The key idea is that a Store machine can find a photo using only the logical volume id and the file offset. The machine keeps open file descriptors for its volumes and an in-memory hash from photo key to (file, offset, size) and flags. Retrieving a photo therefore needs no disk metadata operations before the read itself. After a crash, the Store rebuilds this mapping by scanning the volume files before it serves requests. The slides call this "the keystone of the Haystack design".

Put another way: the in-memory table is what makes each photo cost one disk read. Metadata per photo is about 40 bytes in Haystack, compared with roughly 500 bytes for the Linux xfs inode structure.

10. The Directory and the Cache

The Directory does four jobs. It maps logical volumes to physical volumes. It balances load across logical volumes and spreads reads across physical volumes. It decides whether a CDN or the Cache serves a given photo. And it marks physical volumes as read-only when they are full or for operational reasons. New physical volumes are added as others fill up, and only volumes marked for write accept uploads.

The Cache is a distributed hash table from photo id to photo location, acting as an internal CDN. It caches a photo only when two rules are met: the request comes directly from a user rather than from an external CDN, which suggests the content is new and trending, and the photo was fetched from a machine that accepts uploads. Read-only volumes mostly hold old content, so this rule keeps the cache for new content.

11. Read, write and delete

A browser request goes to the web server, which builds a URL of the form http://<CDN-Name>/<Cache-Name>/<Machine-id>/<Logical Volume, Photo>. The CDN named in the URL serves the request if it can. If not, it strips its part of the URL and forwards to the Cache. If the Cache misses, it forwards to the Store machine named in the URL, which reads the volume at the given offset. The Store checks that the photo is not marked deleted and verifies the cookie. The cookie is a random 32-bit number assigned at upload and embedded in the URL. It stops attackers from guessing valid URLs for denial-of-service attacks.

On upload, the web server passes the logical volume id, key, alternate key, cookie and data to the Store machines. Each machine synchronously appends the needle to its physical volume file and updates its in-memory mapping. Each photo is stored in four sizes under the same key, to cope with different device form factors.

Operations such as rotation create a new needle with the same key and alternate key. If the new needle goes into the same logical volume, it is appended to the same physical volumes, and the Store treats the needle with the larger offset as the newer version. If it goes into a different logical volume, the Directory updates the metadata entries for the original needle.

Delete is logical. The Store sets a delete flag in the in-memory mapping and synchronously in the volume file, so deleted photos are never returned. The space is reclaimed later by compaction. Periodically the machine walks all needles, copies the valid ones to a new file, and switches its in-memory structures to the new file.

12. Other systems

  • Google Colossus is the next version of GFS, designed for much more scale. It uses smaller blocks and more metadata, keeps metadata in a database rather than in memory, and has multiple master nodes. It also marks data as hot (used heavily now, such as photos and news) or cold (old and little used). Each disk should hold a mix of hot and cold data, otherwise some disks are overused and others underused.
  • Facebook Tectonic generalises Haystack. Haystack was mainly for blob storage, while Tectonic supports several application scenarios.
Exam pointers:
  • Why 64 MB chunks, and what the trade-off is (less metadata in memory and less network overhead, but fragmentation for small files).
  • Why the master is kept out of the data path, and why chunk locations are rebuilt from chunkservers rather than stored persistently.
  • Leases: at most one primary per chunk at a time; primary sets the order; record append lets the primary pick the offset, giving at-least-once atomic appends with padding and client retries.
  • Haystack: one disk read per photo because the in-memory index gives the offset; the cookie guards against guessing; deletes are logical and reclaimed by compaction.

Lecture 11: Locating Data, P2P Overlays and Consistent Hashing

Source: Lecture11.pdf, slides 1–24

1. The problem: how do you find a key?

A distributed data store is an abstraction for storing and accessing data on many machines, often commodity ones that also serve data to other users. Data is stored as key-value pairs, and the system needs a way to answer a query: given a key, which machine holds its value? The lecture's reading is Karger et al. (STOC 1997), which is the consistent hashing paper used later in the lecture.

2. Three generations of data sharing

Overlay network An application-level network built on top of the physical network. Its nodes and links define how peers find each other and data. The slides also call structured and unstructured systems "overlays".
  • First generation: limited decentralisation. Servers keep an index file. Napster is the example.
  • Second generation: fully decentralised, peer-to-peer. Peers collaborate to store and locate data. These are either structured or unstructured overlays. Examples: Chord, Tapestry, Gnutella, KaZaA.
  • Third generation: hybrid or enhanced P2P. Adds security, anonymity, censorship resistance, incentive mechanisms and better scalability. Examples: Freenet, Tor, BitTorrent (with a DHT), I2P.

3. Napster: a centralised index

Napster was a search engine for MP3 files. Each user, on connecting, shares the list of MP3s they own with the Napster broker, which keeps the index. A user searches through the broker, but the file transfer goes directly between the client that has the file and the client that wants it. The broker is not involved in the transfer.

The slides note several optimisations: there can be multiple brokers, clients can connect to the least loaded one, and downloads can come from machines inside private networks. The problems were legal (the legality of the sharing service was heavily questioned), and there was no anonymity for anyone. Napster was shut down in 2001 over copyright disputes. The lesson for the exam is that the index is a single point of control and failure, which is what second-generation systems try to remove.

4. Unstructured and structured overlays

Second-generation systems have no central server. Peers share information with each other to locate and download files. There are two strategies:

  • Unstructured overlays have an arbitrary set of connections between nodes. Information spreads by gossip-style protocols, such as rumour spreading or epidemic propagation. These networks follow no regular topology. Search is ad hoc, using variants of flooding and random walk. Gnutella is the example.
  • Structured overlays have well-defined connections, at least logically. They follow a regular topology such as a hypercube, mesh or butterfly. The topology guides how objects are stored and searched, so object placement and search are tied to the overlay structure and data organisation.

Slide 13 lists the general properties of P2P networks. The network is an application-level organisation of nodes that lets them share resources flexibly. All nodes are equal and talk directly to each other, with no client-server split. Any object can be located without a DNS-style service. The network acts like one large combined pool of storage and CPU, and nodes and resources can be inserted and removed cheaply and dynamically.

5. How data is placed: index types

Data is identified by an index, which decouples the physical location of data from the applications that use it. Slide 14 names three kinds of index:

  • Centralised indexing, as in DNS servers.
  • Distributed indexing, where the index is scattered across peers and accessed through mechanisms such as a Distributed Hash Table (DHT). The schemes differ in their hash mapping, search algorithm, lookup diameter, fault tolerance and churn resilience.
  • Local indexing, where each peer indexes only its own objects. Remote objects must be searched for, usually by flooding or random walk. This is common in unstructured overlays such as Gnutella.

Slide 15 gives a second classification: semantic versus semantic-free indexing. Semantic indexes are human-readable (a filename, a keyword, a database key) and support keyword, range and approximate searches. Semantic-free indexes are not human-readable. They come from a good hash function, which helps the search process.

6. Why plain hashing fails when caches change

Slides 16 and 17 set up the motivation. A single server holds many objects, and caches are used to speed it up. We want objects spread evenly across the caches, so each cache has a near-equal share. Clients must also know which cache holds a given object. Hashing solves both needs: the server and the clients use the same hash function, so a client can compute which cache to ask.

The drawback comes when the set of caches changes. Suppose the hash is modulo p, for example f(x) = ax + b (mod p), where p is the number of machines. When machines are added or removed, the range p changes, and almost every item hashes to a new location. Slide 19 says this directly.

7. Consistent hashing

The fix is consistent hashing. Define a view as the set of buckets a particular client is aware of. Different clients can have different views. For example, one client sees {B2, B6, B7} and another sees {B1, B3, B5}. A key question is what happens when clients disagree about which buckets exist.

A consistent hash family has three properties (slides 21 to 23):

  • Smoothness. When a machine is added or removed, the expected fraction of objects that must move is the minimum needed to keep the load balanced.
  • Spread. Across all client views, the total number of different caches to which one object is assigned must be small.
  • Load. The number of distinct objects assigned to any one cache must be small.

Slide 22 gives a worked example. Object x = 12 is hashed under four views. H(12, V1) = 1, H(12, V2) = 4, H(12, V3) = 1, H(12, V4) = 2. V1 and V3 are the same view, so they agree. Over all views the object goes to buckets {1, 2, 4}, so its spread is 3.

Slide 24 explains what the properties mean in practice. Smoothness means that small changes in the set of caches require only small changes in where objects live. Spread means that even when clients have inconsistent views, requests for an object go to only a few caches. Load means each cache gets almost the same number of objects. The slide ends with the question "Do such hashing schemes exist?". Lecture 12 answers it with ranged hash functions.

Exam pointers:
  • Why modulo hashing breaks: changing p remaps almost every item. Know the three consistent-hashing properties (smoothness, spread, load) and what each one guarantees.
  • Structured versus unstructured overlays: a regular topology guides storage and search, while unstructured overlays use flooding or random walk.
  • Napster as a first-generation system: its central index and the shutdown reason.
  • Index types: centralised, distributed (DHT) and local; semantic versus semantic-free.

Lecture 12: Ranged Hashing, Consistent Hashing and Chord

Source: Lecture12.pdf, slides 1–25

Note: the slide text lost several mathematical symbols (subset, membership, and the spread and load symbols). Where a formula is unclear, this guide uses the standard form from the Karger et al. paper (background), and says so.

1. Setting up ranged hash functions

Lecture 11 ended with the question "do such hashing schemes exist?". Lecture 12 gives the construction. Let I be the set of items and B the set of buckets. A view V is any subset of B. A ranged hash function is a function f : 2B × I → B. For each possible view it assigns every item to a bucket. We write fV(i) for the bucket that item i goes to in view V. A family of such functions is a ranged hash family. A random ranged hash function is one drawn uniformly at random from the family.

The idea is that each client has its own view, and each view yields a placement. The three properties below measure how good a family is.

2. Balance

A family is balanced if, for a given view V, a set of items and a randomly chosen function, the fraction of items mapped to each bucket is O(1/|V|) with high probability. Random functions in the family therefore spread items evenly among the buckets of the view.

3. Monotonicity

Monotone function f is monotone if, for views V1 ⊆ V2 ⊆ B, whenever fV2(i) ∈ V1, then fV1(i) = fV2(i). A family is monotone if every function in it is monotone.

In words: if buckets are added to a view, an item may move from an old bucket to a new one, but never from one old bucket to another old bucket. The slide's intuition is that when the set of usable buckets changes, items should move only when needed to keep the distribution even.

4. Spread

Spread is about disagreement between clients. Take a set of views V1, ..., Vv that together contain C distinct buckets, with each view containing at least C/t buckets. For an item i, the spread is the number of distinct buckets {fVj(i)} over all the views. The spread of a function is the maximum spread over all items. The spread of a family is small if, with high probability, a random function from it has small spread. Intuitively, there are v people, each of whom sees a constant fraction (1/t) of the buckets, and each tries to place the item with a consistent hash. Spread counts how many different opinions there are across the group. A good function has low spread for every item.

Worked example from slide 6: v = 4 views, and item i = 12 is placed as f(12, V1) = 1, f(12, V2) = 4, f(12, V3) = 1, f(12, V4) = 2. The distinct buckets are {1, 4, 2}, so spread(12) = 3.

5. Load

Load looks at buckets rather than items. Write f-1V(b) for the set of items assigned to bucket b in view V. The load of bucket b is the number of distinct items that at least one view assigns to b, that is the size of the union over the views of f-1V(b). The load of a function is the maximum load over buckets. A family has small load if a random function has small load with high probability.

Slide 10 says load is similar to spread, but for a bucket instead of an item. The load bound counts the distinct items that at least one view thinks belong in the bucket. A good consistent hash function also has low load.

6. A construction with a ring

The construction is simple. Take two random functions, rB and rI. rB maps buckets uniformly into the unit interval [0, 1], and rI does the same for items. An item i is assigned to the bucket b in view V that is closest to rI(i) in the distance along the ring. Think of the interval as a circle: buckets and items are points on it, and each item goes to the nearest bucket that is in the current view.

For analysis, each bucket is mapped to several points on the ring. If the number of buckets is always less than C, each bucket gets k log C points for some constant k. This is like replicating each bucket about k log C times, and it smooths out the placement.

Slide 13 gives the result: this construction is a ranged hash family that is monotone, has spread O(log C) and load O(log C), both with high probability. C is the number of buckets. The proof relies on Chernoff bounds and on the independence of rB and rI. The slides defer the details to the paper.

7. Chord: consistent hashing for lookup

Chord is the first structured overlay example. It uses consistent hashing. Node addresses and object keys are both mapped into one common identifier space. Locating an object has two steps: map the object's value to its key, then map the key to the node that stores it, using a lookup.

Placement. The identifier space is m-bit, with 2m addresses, arranged as a logical ring mod 2m. A key k is assigned to the first node whose identifier is equal to or greater than k. This node is called the successor of k.

Basic lookup. Each node tracks its successor on the ring. A query for key x is forwarded around the ring until it reaches the first node whose identifier is at least the key. The result travels back along the reverse of the path. This needs only O(1) local state per node, but takes O(n) hops. Slides 16 to 20 have identical text: they are animation builds of the same search-path diagram.

Improved lookup with finger tables. Each node i keeps a routing table called the finger table with O(log n) entries. The j-th entry is the node succ((i + 2j-1) mod 2m), that is the first node at least 2j-1 ahead of i. On a unit ring with node i in [0, 1), the j-th finger sits at position i + 2j-1-m, or at the successor of that point if no node is there.

Lookup then behaves like a binary search. A node first contacts the finger for j = 1. If that node does not hold the object, the search continues through the next finger, and so on. The cost is O(log n) message hops, paid for with O(log n) space in each node's routing table.

8. Churn: joins and leaves

When a new node joins, it must: find its predecessor and successor; take ownership of the items that now map to it; and build its finger table. It can build the finger table by using the finger table of its successor. When a node leaves, it must: inform its predecessor and successor, and transfer the items it owns to its successor.

9. Other structured overlays

The slide closes by naming other structured overlay models: CAN (Content Addressable Network) and Tapestry, with "many more" left unnamed. Chord is the one studied in detail in this lecture.

Exam pointers:
  • Know the three properties of a ranged hash family and what each one bounds: balance (items per bucket), monotonicity (items move only into new buckets), spread (distinct buckets across views, the disagreement count), load (distinct items per bucket).
  • The ring construction gives monotone, spread O(log C), load O(log C) with high probability.
  • Chord placement: the key goes to its successor on an m-bit ring. Basic lookup is O(1) space and O(n) hops; finger tables give O(log n) space and O(log n) hops.
  • Finger j of node i is succ(i + 2j-1), and churn requires updating the predecessor, successor, items and finger tables.

Lecture 14: Distributed Consensus and Crash Failures

Source: Lecture14.pdf, slides 1–29

The problem

The slides open with a hiring story. Four interviewers meet one candidate separately, each forms a local yes/no view, and then the four must reach one common decision. This is the classical distributed consensus problem. The same problem appears in distributed database commit/abort decisions, in agreeing on the reading reported by different sensors, and in air traffic control, where all aircraft must hold the same view.

System model

  • There are n processes. Every pair has a logical channel, and these channels are assumed reliable.
  • Messages are not authenticated. Contents can be garbled or forged. Only the sender's id is trustworthy.
  • Timing is considered in two separate cases: synchronous and asynchronous. In an asynchronous system, if a message from Pi to Pj does not arrive, Pj cannot tell a lost message from a slow one.
  • Failures can be fail-stop, Byzantine, or others. A process with a reason to influence the hiring decision is modelled as a faulty process.

Formal definitions

Consensus. Each process starts with an initial value. The conditions are: Agreement (all non-faulty processes decide the same value), Validity (if all non-faulty processes start with the same value, that is the decided value), and Termination (every non-faulty process eventually decides).

The validity condition rules out trivial solutions, such as always deciding a fixed default value. Faulty processes may or may not decide, and their decisions are ignored.

Distributed agreement. One designated source process starts with a value. The conditions are the same as above, except validity: if the source is non-faulty, every non-faulty process must decide the source's initial value.

The slides show that the two problems are equivalent and can be reduced to each other. The difference is only where the initial values are: in consensus every node has one, and in agreement only the initiator has one. Solutions in both cases are judged by the same three properties.

The grid to keep in mind

The lecture builds one table, with rows for synchronous and asynchronous systems and columns for fault-free, crash (fail-stop), and Byzantine faults. The final state, after Lectures 14 and 15, is:

ModelFault-freeCrash (fail-stop)Byzantine
SynchronousEasy, all-to-all communicationf+1 roundsPossible if n > 3f with O(nf) messages (exponential algorithm); with O(n²f) messages if n > 4f (Phase King)
AsynchronousPossible, but deferred. Lecture 15 shows that crash and Byzantine consensus are impossible.

The fault-free case

If no process fails, each process broadcasts its value to all others (an all-to-all broadcast). Everyone then computes the same function, such as min, max, average, or majority, over the n values. In a synchronous network this takes a constant number of rounds. The asynchronous fault-free case is postponed to a later lecture.

Crash failures: the fail-stop model

In the fail-stop (crash) model a process can stop at any moment, even halfway through a send or receive step. There are n processes, up to f of which may be faulty. Values are integers here.

The algorithm ConsensusFailStop

Each process Pi starts with xi. Then the algorithm runs for f+1 rounds:

  1. If xi has not been sent yet, broadcast xi to all other processes.
  2. Receive the values yj sent by the other processes.
  3. Set xi = min(xi, min over j of yj).

After f+1 rounds, Pi outputs xi as the consensus value. (The slide 18 wording says a process sends again only if its value changed in the previous round. Slide 19 says a value is sent only if it has not been sent yet. Both give the same behaviour: a value is sent once.)

Worked example

Five nodes start with (1, 1, 0, 1, 1). With no failures the answer should be 0. Assume P3, the only holder of 0, is the faulty node.

  • P3 crashes in round 1 after sending 0 to P2 only. P2 takes min(1, 0) = 0. Everyone else still sees 1 and keeps 1. In round 2 P3 is silent, but P2 still holds an unsent 0, so it broadcasts 0. Everyone updates to 0, and the result is 0.
  • P3 crashes before sending anything. The system behaves like four nodes with values 1, 1, 1, 1. The only value anyone learns is 1, so the result is 1. This is still valid, because the faulty node's value was never seen.

The example shows that the output depends on what the failed process managed to send, but every run still ends with one common value.

Why the algorithm is correct

Agreement. There are f+1 rounds and at most f crashes, so at least one round r has no failures. In round r every non-faulty process broadcasts its current value, and every other process takes the minimum over them. Call that minimum v. After round r, only v can still be broadcast, and it can be sent at most one more time.

Validity. A crashing process only sends correct values up to the round where it fails, so it never spreads a wrong value. If every process starts with the same v, then v is the only value ever sent.

Termination. The algorithm stops after f+1 rounds, so every non-faulty process decides.

Complexity and lower bound

  • Rounds: f+1.
  • Messages per round: O(n²), since each of up to n processes sends to all others.
  • Total messages: O(f·n²). The slides say this bound is tight, with an example where one process fails after sending to exactly one other process in each of rounds 1 to f.
  • Lower bound: if there are f faults, f+1 rounds are needed in the worst case. The example is one crash in every round.
Exam pointers:
  • Know the difference between consensus (every node has an initial value) and agreement (only the source has one), and that the two reduce to each other.
  • State the three properties: Agreement, Validity, Termination. Be ready to explain why validity rules out a fixed default answer.
  • Trace the fail-stop algorithm on the (1, 1, 0, 1, 1) example and explain why f+1 rounds guarantee one clean round.
  • Know the complexity: f+1 rounds, O(f·n²) messages, and why the bound is tight.

Lecture 15: Phase King, the FLP Result, and Paxos

Source: Lecture15.pdf, slides 1–38

Where we are

Lecture 14 solved crash-failure consensus in synchronous systems with f+1 rounds. This lecture makes the Byzantine synchronous case cheaper in messages, then looks at asynchronous systems. The summary table after slide 16 reads: a synchronous system with Byzantine faults is possible if n > 3f with O(nf) messages (the exponential algorithm from the previous lecture), and possible with O(n²f) messages if n > 4f (the Phase King algorithm below). Asynchronous consensus is impossible under crash or Byzantine faults.

Note: the slides say the earlier algorithm uses O(nf) messages in the table but an exponential number of messages in the text on slide 3. The exponential count is the correct one (see the Byzantine lecture notes).

Phase King: polynomial message size

The earlier algorithm needs an exponential number of messages. Phase King keeps messages short and polynomial by trading away some processes. It needs n > 4f processors, runs for f+1 phases, and each phase takes two rounds, so there are 2(f+1) rounds in total.

The algorithm

Each processor Pi keeps a preference pref, which starts as its input. In phase k (k from 1 to f+1), Pk is the king.

  1. Round 1 of phase k. Send pref to all. Receive the prefs from everyone. Let majority be the value that appears more than n/2 times (0 if none). Let multiplicity be how many times that majority value appears.
  2. Round 2 of phase k. The king Pk sends its majority to all, and this is the tie-breaker. Every processor receives the tie-breaker from Pk (0 if none). Then: if multiplicity > n/2 + f, set pref to majority. Otherwise set pref to the tie-breaker.
  3. After phase f+1, decide pref.

The rule is that a processor trusts its own majority only when it is very strong (more than n/2 + f copies). Otherwise it follows the king. Since there are f+1 phases and at most f faulty kings, at least one king is honest.

Worked example: n = 9, f = 2

Processors P1 to P9. P6 and P7 are Byzantine. The honest initial values are P1=1, P2=1, P3=1, P4=0, P5=0, P8=1, and P9=0. The threshold n/2 + f is 6 on the slides (n/2 = 4.5, so the exact test is multiplicity of at least 7; the examples below come out the same either way).

  • Phase 1 (king P1). In round 1 the faulty processors send different values to different honest processors, so P1 sees five 1s and four 0s. The majority is 1 with multiplicity 5, which is not above the threshold. P1 sends 1 as the tie-breaker, and everyone who is not faulty follows it.
  • Phase 2 (king P2). Now P6 and P7 send 0 to everyone. The honest processors send 1, so every honest processor sees seven 1s. The multiplicity of 7 is above the threshold, so every honest processor keeps 1 without needing the king.
  • Phase 3 (king P3). The honest processors still send 1 and the faulty ones still send 0, so the multiplicity is again above the threshold. At the end of the phase all honest processors (P1 to P5, P8, P9) prefer 1 and output 1.

Slide 8 is labelled "Phase 1 — King is P3". That label is a copy error for phase 3.

Why Phase King works

Unanimous Phase Lemma. If all non-faulty processors prefer v at the start of phase k, they all prefer v at the end. Each one receives at least n − f votes for v in round 1. Since n > 4f, n − f > n/2 + f, so every non-faulty processor sees multiplicity above the threshold and keeps v.
Validity. If all processors start with v, they all prefer v from the first phase on, by the unanimous phase lemma. After phase f+1 they all decide v.
Non-faulty King Lemma. If the king Pk of phase k is non-faulty, then all non-faulty processors have the same preference at the end of phase k. There are three cases:
  • Both Pi and Pj take the king's tie-breaker. The king is non-faulty, so both get the same value.
  • Pi uses its majority v (more than n/2 + f votes for v), and Pj uses the tie-breaker. Pk then sees more than n/2 votes for v, so its tie-breaker is v. Pj therefore also gets v.
  • Both use their own majorities. If Pi's majority is v, then Pj sees more than n/2 votes for v, so Pj's majority is also v.
Agreement. There are f+1 phases, and at most f are faulty, so one king is non-faulty. By the non-faulty king lemma, all non-faulty processors agree at the end of that phase. By the unanimous phase lemma, they stay in agreement for every later phase. So all non-faulty decisions match.

Summary. n > 4f; 2(f+1) rounds; O(n²f) messages.

The FLP result

Fischer, Lynch and Paterson showed that in an asynchronous system, consensus is impossible even with a single crash fault. The nature of the fault does not matter. The slides call this the FLP result and leave the proof as a reading exercise. The consequence is serious, because most practical systems are asynchronous, and tasks such as leader election become impossible in that model. Yet real distributed databases do use consensus-style protocols, so there is a middle ground. Paxos is one example.

Paxos: the setting

  • A set of processes can propose values.
  • Processes can crash and recover, and they have access to stable storage.
  • Communication is asynchronous. Messages can be lost or duplicated, but not corrupted.

Two conditions must hold. Safety (equal to validity): only a proposed value can be chosen, only one value is chosen, and a process never learns a value was chosen unless it really was. Liveness (equal to agreement plus termination): some proposed value is eventually chosen, and if a value is chosen, a process eventually learns it.

Paxos has three roles: proposers, acceptors, and learners.

Building Paxos up

  • One acceptor. It picks the value from all proposals. This works until it fails. Nobody else knows the choice, so it is centralised and not good enough.
  • Several acceptors, choose by majority. A value is chosen only when a majority of acceptors accept it. Two majorities always overlap, so at most one value is chosen.
  • Rule R1. An acceptor must accept the first proposal it receives. This handles a single proposer, and also an acceptor that has just recovered. With several proposers each proposing a different value, R1 alone is not enough.
  • Numbered proposals. Acceptors must accept more than one proposal. Each proposal is a pair (psn, value), where psn is a natural number and different proposals have different psn. A proposal is chosen when a majority accepts it, and a value is chosen when one proposal with that value is chosen.
  • Rule R2. If a proposal with value v is chosen, every higher-numbered proposal that is chosen has value v. This is enforced through R2a (every higher-numbered proposal accepted by any acceptor has value v), and then the tighter R2b: every higher-numbered proposal issued by any proposer has value v.

The two-phase protocol

  1. Prepare. A proposer picks a new n and sends <Prepare, n, v> to a majority of acceptors. An acceptor that receives a prepare with n' greater than any prepare it has answered promises not to accept any proposal numbered below n'. It replies with the highest-numbered proposal it has already accepted, if any.
  2. Accept. If the proposer gets replies from a majority, it sends <Accept, n, v> to all acceptors. Here v is the value of the highest-numbered proposal among the replies, or any value if no proposal was reported. An acceptor accepts unless it has since answered a prepare with a number greater than n.

The acceptor's rules: it always answers a prepare. It answers an accept with number n only if it has not answered a prepare with a number greater than n. Lower-numbered requests get no reply at all.

Quick example with five nodes

All of P1 to P5 can be acceptors and proposers. Each keeps promised_seq (the highest number promised) and (accepted_seq, accepted_val), all starting at 0 and null.

  • P1 sends <Prepare, 5, a>. Everyone except P2 replies <OK, 5, a>. P1 has a majority of promises but has not yet sent Accept.
  • Before that Accept goes out, P2 sends <Prepare, 8, b>. Since 8 > 5, the others are free to answer OK. P2 can then send Accept with value b.
  • P1 sees this and sends a new prepare with number 10. Any proposer whose prepare number is below 8 (or 10) gets no OK replies.

Proposals from P1 and P2 can keep leapfrogging each other forever. The value is not what drives progress here; the number is. The slides note that value is only needed for validity, and values need not increase. So safety holds, but liveness fails.

Liveness and the leader

Paxos as described does not guarantee progress. Two proposers can keep making higher proposals that are never accepted. The fix is to have only one active proposer at a time. In normal operation, a single server is elected as leader and acts as the distinguished proposer.

How Paxos gets around FLP

Paxos is always safe. For progress it needs a leader, but leader election is hard in an asynchronous system. So Paxos does not contradict FLP. If there are enough periods of synchrony, Paxos is both safe and live.

Exam pointers:
  • Phase King: n > 4f, 2(f+1) rounds, O(n²f) messages. Know the two rounds of a phase and the test multiplicity > n/2 + f.
  • Know the three lemmas (unanimous phase, validity, non-faulty king) and how agreement follows from them.
  • FLP: consensus is impossible in asynchronous systems even with one crash fault.
  • Paxos: safety always, liveness needs a single leader and periods of synchrony. Know the roles and rules R1, R2 (R2a, R2b), and the prepare/accept steps.

Lecture 15: Byzantine Agreement in Synchronous Systems

Source: ByzantineConsensus.pdf, slides 1–28

Starting point

The summary table from the earlier lecture has one open cell, Byzantine faults in a synchronous system. This deck fills it in. Byzantine faults are arbitrary: a faulty process may send different values to different processes, or relay wrong information. This is harder than crash failures, where a process only stops.

The generals story

The name comes from the Byzantine empire. Invading armies are split into groups, each led by a general, and they attack from several directions. The attack succeeds only if all groups attack at the same time, so the generals must agree on the attack time. A general who is a traitor is modelled as a faulty process. The only way the generals can communicate is by messengers, which here means messages. A Byzantine general can tell different groups different attack times, or pass on wrong reports.

The problem of reaching agreement under these conditions is the Byzantine agreement problem. Its properties are those from the consensus lecture: agreement among non-faulty processes, validity when the source is non-faulty, and termination.

Impossibility with 3 nodes and 1 fault

Notation: n is the number of nodes, f is the number of faulty nodes. The network is synchronous and fully connected. The smallest example is S(3,1), with n = 3 and f = 1. Let Pc be the initiator with value 0, and let Pa and Pb be the other nodes.

Suppose Pa is faulty. In round 1, Pc sends 0 to Pa and Pb. In round 2, Pa tells Pb 1 while Pb tells Pa 0. Pb has no way to know whether Pa or Pc is at fault. The same confusion appears if Pc is the faulty one.

The problem is that Pb receives the same inputs in two scenarios that need different outputs. If Pa is faulty, validity forces Pb and Pc to output 0, since Pc started with 0. If Pc is faulty, Pa and Pb must still output the same value. Pb cannot tell the scenarios apart, so the two requirements clash. The conclusion is that with one faulty node among three, agreement is impossible even in a synchronous system.

The result extends to any n with f at least n/3. The argument is a reduction. Split the n nodes of S(n, f) into three sets S1, S2, S3 of size n/3 (assuming n is divisible by 3). Each node of S(3,1) simulates one of the sets. A single faulty node in S(3,1) then corresponds to n/3 faulty nodes in S(n, f). An agreement algorithm for S(n, f) with f ≥ n/3 would give one for S(3,1), which is impossible. So the bigger system is impossible too.

An algorithm for S(4,1)

Here f = 1 is less than n/3, so agreement is possible. The algorithm has two rounds:

  1. The initiator sends its value to all other nodes. That is n − 1 messages.
  2. Every other node relays the value it received from the initiator to all other nodes. That is (n − 1)(n − 2) messages. Each node then takes the majority of all the values it has.

Why two rounds? Round 1 is simply the initiator's broadcast. With at most one fault in S(4,1), each node relays what it heard, and the majority washes out the effect of the one faulty node. Two rounds are needed to tolerate one fault. Each node's action in round 2 can be viewed as a separate subproblem on a smaller system, S(n−1, f−1).

Seven nodes with two faults

Consider seven nodes with two faults. P0 is the initiator and is faulty. It sends 0 to P1 through P4, and 1 to the others.

Look at P3. It receives 0 from P0. In round 2, every node P1 to P6 relays what it received from P0. Suppose P4 is also faulty. It sends 1 to P3 and 0 to everyone else. P3 relays 0 to everyone except P0 and itself.

Majority is not enough at this point. P3 cannot tell that 0 is the true value and that the 1s are from faulty nodes, especially when the source itself is faulty. Different honest nodes can end up with different majority values after round 2. That is not a valid consensus.

In round 3 each node, except P0, sends (n−2)(n−3) messages that convey what it heard from others in round 2. This extra round gives every node a second look at the relayed values, so the faulty reports can be filtered out.

General algorithm

With more nodes and more faults, the idea is to use f+1 rounds to wash out the effect of all f faulty nodes. In each round, every node acts as the initiator of a distinct subsystem S(ni, fi), with ni = n − i and fi = f − i.

The message count across the rounds follows the recurrence M(n, f) = (n − 1) · M(n − 1, f − 1), with M(n, 1) = n − 1. Unrolling it gives the product (n − 1)(n − 2)…. The slide ends the product at (n − f − 1) and calls the total O(nf). This is a slip. Unrolling the recurrence ends at (n − f), and a product of f factors each near n is O(n^f), which is exponential in f. Lecture 15 also says the earlier algorithm needs an exponential number of messages.

Why it works. If the initiator is non-faulty, it sends the same value to everyone. All non-faulty processes then hold the same value, and the later rounds preserve that. If the initiator is malicious and sends 0 to half the nodes and 1 to the other half, the non-faulty nodes do not start with the same view. The extra rounds let the non-faulty nodes reach one value. The condition that makes this work is (n − f)/2 > f, so that one half of the non-faulty nodes can impose its majority on the whole set of non-faulty nodes. This simplifies to n > 3f. The algorithm then tolerates up to f faults.

Exam pointers:
  • Why n = 3, f = 1 is impossible: a node cannot tell which of two parties is faulty, and validity forces two different outputs. Know the reduction that extends it to f ≥ n/3.
  • S(4,1) algorithm: two rounds, majority of relayed values. Know why the second round is needed.
  • General algorithm: f+1 rounds, the n > 3f condition, and the message count. Note the slide's O(nf) is a typo for O(n^f).

Lecture 18: Transactions, Nested Transactions and Atomic Commit

Source: Lecture18-Databases1.pdf, slides 1–41

What a transaction is (slides 2–4)

A client often needs a sequence of requests to one server to be atomic: no other client's operations should interleave with them, and if the server crashes, either all of the operations are completed or none of them has any effect. The slides state the goal as keeping every object at a server in a consistent state when several transactions access it, even across crashes.

The scope is limited. Transactions handle crash failures of processes and omission failures in communication. They do not handle arbitrary (Byzantine) behaviour. Lampson's fault model, which the slides mention, covers failures of disks, servers and communication.

ACID (slides 5–13)

The desirable properties of a transaction are summarised by the mnemonic ACID, which Härder and Reuter proposed.

Atomicity A transaction is all or nothing.
Consistency A transaction takes the system from one consistent state to another consistent state.
Isolation Each transaction runs without interference from other transactions.
Durability Once a transaction has completed successfully, its effects are saved in permanent storage.

A transaction ends in one of two ways: it commits, or it is aborted. Either the client aborts it or the server aborts it.

Nested transactions (slides 14–16, 22)

Transactions can be nested. A top-level transaction can start subtransactions, and each subtransaction can start more. The slides use a holiday booking on a travel website as the example. Flights, ground transport, meals, activities and hotels are handled by different agencies, and each may have its own steps.

The commit rules for nested transactions are:

  1. A transaction can commit or abort only after all its child transactions have completed.
  2. When a subtransaction completes, it decides independently to commit provisionally or to abort. An abort decision is final.
  3. If a parent aborts, all its subtransactions abort.
  4. If a subtransaction aborts, the parent decides whether to abort too.
  5. If the top-level transaction commits, the provisionally committed subtransactions can commit too, provided none of their ancestors has aborted.

Ways to handle concurrency (slide 17)

The slides list three approaches: locks, timestamp ordering, and optimistic concurrency control. They are only named here. The slides point to the Kindberg et al. book for details.

Distributed transactions and the coordinator (slides 18–20, 23–24)

A distributed transaction accesses objects on several servers. Atomicity then requires that either all the servers commit or all of them abort. One server acts as the coordinator to make sure every server reaches the same outcome. The slides use a UPI payment for a canteen tea as the example. The debit happens at one bank and the credit at another, and both must happen together.

The client starts a transaction by sending openTransaction to a coordinator. The coordinator returns a transaction identifier (TID), which must be unique across the whole distributed system. The coordinator that opened the transaction is responsible for committing or aborting it at the end. Every server that manages an object the transaction touches is a participant. Participants cooperate with the coordinator in the commit protocol.

Flat versus nested (slides 21–22)

In a flat transaction the client calls one server after another, and each request finishes before the next begins. With locking, a flat transaction waits for at most one object at a time.

In a nested transaction, subtransactions at the same level can run concurrently. In the slide's example, T1 and T2 run in parallel, and so do the four leaves T11, T12, T21 and T22.

Atomic commit protocols (slides 25–33)

A one-phase protocol would have the coordinator send commit or abort to every participant and keep repeating until all acknowledge. The slides say this is not enough. It does not let a server refuse to commit when the client asks for a commit. Reasons a server may need to abort are:

  • deadlock resolution in its concurrency control,
  • failed validation under optimistic concurrency control,
  • the coordinator not knowing that a server crashed and was replaced.

Two-phase commit (2PC) lets any participant abort its part. The key rule is that once a participant votes Yes, it may never abort. Before voting Yes, it must save every object it changed, together with its status prepared, in permanent storage. A prepared participant can then commit even if it crashes and is replaced.

The decision rule is simple: if any participant votes No, the outcome is abort. If all vote Yes, the outcome is commit. The difficulty is making sure all participants vote and agree, even when servers crash, messages are lost, or servers cannot reach each other.

The model assumes an asynchronous system where servers can crash and messages can be lost. A request-reply layer removes corrupt and duplicate messages. There are no Byzantine faults, so servers either crash or obey what they are sent. The slides also say 2PC reaches consensus in this setting, even though consensus is impossible in an asynchronous system with failures in general. The reason given is that a crashed process is replaced by a new one that loads its state from permanent storage and from the other processes.

The two phases (slides 34–36)

Phase 1 (voting).

  1. The coordinator sends canCommit? to each participant.
  2. Each participant replies Yes or No.
  3. Before voting Yes, it prepares by saving its objects in permanent storage.
  4. A participant that votes No aborts immediately.

Phase 2 (completion). The coordinator collects all the votes, including its own.

  • If there are no failures and every vote is Yes, it decides commit and sends doCommit to every participant.
  • Otherwise it decides abort and sends doAbort to the participants that voted Yes.
  • A participant that receives the decision acts on it. After a commit it sends haveCommitted back to the coordinator.

Timeouts and failure cases (slides 37–40)

  • Participant that voted Yes. It is uncertain and cannot proceed until it learns the outcome. It can send getDecision to the coordinator. If the coordinator has failed, it must wait until the coordinator is replaced, which can cause long delays.
  • Participant that has not yet been asked to vote. It may have finished its client requests but has not received canCommit?. Since no decision exists yet, it can abort unilaterally, after noticing that no request has arrived for a long time.
  • Coordinator waiting for votes. It may abort after a timeout by sending doAbort to participants that have voted. A late Yes vote is ignored, and that participant enters the uncertain state.

Cost (slide 41)

With N participants, 2PC uses N canCommit? messages with N replies, followed by N doCommit messages. That is about 4N messages and four rounds. The protocol tolerates a series of failures and is guaranteed to finish eventually. The slides stress that no time limit can be given for when it will finish.

Exam pointers:
  • Know the four ACID properties and what each guarantees.
  • Know the 2PC steps. Any No vote means abort. A Yes vote binds the participant to the outcome, so it must save its state as prepared first.
  • Know the uncertain-state problem. A participant that voted Yes must wait for the coordinator, and this is why 2PC can block.
  • Know the message cost: about 4N messages and four rounds.
  • For nested transactions, know the five commit rules. In particular, a parent's abort forces all its children to abort.

Lecture 17: Nested 2PC, Commit Optimisations and NoSQL Trade-offs

Source: Lecture19-Databases2.pdf, slides 1–32

Note: the slide header prints "Lecture 17", but the file is named Lecture19-Databases2. The content is a continuation of two-phase commit (2PC) from the previous lecture.

Recap of 2PC cost (slide 2)

With N participants, 2PC needs N canCommit? messages with N replies, then N doCommit messages. It is designed to survive a series of failures and is guaranteed to finish eventually, though no time limit can be given. The figure below shows the message timeline again, since the slides use it as the standard reference.

2PC for nested transactions (slides 3–6)

The outermost transaction is the top-level transaction. All others are subtransactions. A subtransaction decides for itself, when it finishes, whether to commit provisionally or abort. Once all subtransactions are done, the provisionally committed ones take part in a 2PC. In that round, the servers of provisionally committed subtransactions state their intention to commit. Any server whose ancestor has aborted will abort.

The slides compare two shapes of the protocol:

  • Hierarchical 2PC. The 2PC becomes a multi-level nested protocol. The top-level coordinator sends canCommit? to the coordinators of its immediate subtransactions. Each of those passes the message to its own children, and so on down the tree. Each participant collects the replies from its descendants before replying to its parent.
  • Flat 2PC. The top-level coordinator sends canCommit? directly to the coordinators of every subtransaction on the provisional-commit list.

Isolation and recovery (slide 7)

For isolation, use locks, but be careful about distributed deadlocks. For recovery, use logs so that a server can resume from any state of the 2PC. The slides note that the logging model can be extended to nested transactions.

Optimisations: read-only transactions (slides 8–9)

Mohan et al. proposed two optimisations to 2PC, called presumed abort and presumed commit. The slides name them but this lecture does not explain them. (background) Presumed abort means that a coordinator with no record of a transaction answers abort, so it does not need to log aborts. The slides go on to the read-only case instead.

Partially read-only transaction Some of its processes make no database updates while others do.
Completely read-only transaction No process makes any update.

The read-only rule works as follows. If a subordinate gets a PREPARE and has made no updates, it sends a READ VOTE, releases its locks and forgets the transaction. It writes no log records, and it does not matter to it whether the transaction later commits or aborts. The coordinator then knows this subordinate is read-only, so it does not send it COMMIT or ABORT. If every participant only sends READ VOTEs, there is no second phase at all.

Relational versus non-relational (slides 10–14)

NoSQL systems were built for distributed, very large data. They have a looser schema, are written for specific kinds of data such as documents, and are programmed against the schema rather than the data. They give up strong support for ad hoc queries in exchange for speed and growth. Their query language is the API. They also relax the ACID properties.

AspectRDBMSNoSQL
ScalingScale up: a bigger load needs a bigger serverScale out: data is spread across many hosts
AdministrationNeeds a highly trained DBALess management, automatic repair, simpler data models
Data modelChanges to the schema must be carefully managedLooser structure; schema changes are not one large change unit
EconomicsExpensive proprietary serversClusters of cheap commodity servers; cost per GB or per transaction/s can be lower
SupportStrong vendor support and reputationMostly open-source projects with start-up backing; reputation still forming
MaturityMature, stable, dependable (but not cutting edge)Still implementing basic feature sets
SkillsLarge workforce of experienced developersStill recruiting developers

ACID versus BASE (slides 15, 24)

RDBMSs follow ACID. NoSQL systems often follow BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent. The database is always available. Its state is called soft. The slides do not define this further. (background: copies may disagree for a while until they sync.) Consistency is reached eventually because other mechanisms run in the background. Partitioned databases therefore use BASE to gain availability.

Scaling and partitioning (slides 16–17)

Vertical scaling means using the best single machine available. It is hard to maintain. Horizontal scaling spreads work over many machines, and this raises the question of how to partition the data. The two options are:

  • Functional partitioning. Tables are grouped by function, for example user data in one place, e-transaction data in another, and inventory in a third.
  • Sharding. The whole database is split into pieces, and each piece lives on one server. Functional partitioning can use sharding at a second level if one function's data is too large.

Worked example: a marketplace with Users and eTransactions (slides 18–24)

The example has two tables. eTransactions has one row per sale. Users stores each user's totals, amount_sold and amount_bought. The slides argue that consistency across functional groups is easier to relax than consistency inside one group.

  1. ACID version. One transaction inserts the eTransaction row and updates both users' totals. Both totals are a cache of the transaction table, so their freshness can be relaxed. Users can accept a short delay before their running balance shows a sale.
  2. Two-transaction version. If the insert and the updates are split into two transactions, a failure between them leaves the Users table permanently inconsistent.
  3. Queue version. The insert also queues two messages, one for the seller and one for the buyer. A background loop takes each message and applies it in its own transaction. The queue must be persistent so updates are not lost.
  4. Remaining problem. The message may be in the queue while its transaction is not yet committed, because of 2PC rules. Two fixes are offered: make each update idempotent, or record the applied updates separately and check each new update against that list.

The slides conclude that this gives up a bit of consistency. The database stays available, its state is soft, and it becomes eventually consistent.

Decoupling in a payment (slides 25–26)

A UPI payment has three steps: debit the user, credit the vendor, and insert an audio alert record. In principle all three belong to one transaction. The slides treat them as three subtransactions. If the credit and debit are ready but the queue entry fails, and the parent requires all three, the whole thing aborts. The user then suffers a service disruption for a minor reason, so decoupling the alert is preferred.

Design space of distributed databases (slides 27–32)

  • Data representation. Relational models bring normalisation, integrity constraints, foreign keys and joins. They are harder to partition and scale. Key-value pairs are free-form and easy to partition, scale and cache, but they cannot handle complex transactions or queries.
  • Transaction support. The options range from none for multi-row transactions, to limited support, which is single-row or only within one partition. The hurdles are the inability to reach commit or abort decisions across partitions, and the lack of a consistent clock.
  • Replication and partitioning. Partitioning is needed to scale. Replication handles availability, and it brings challenges for updates, consistency and location.
  • Consistency policy.
    • Updates at an active location only. One replica is active. Updates are sent to passive replicas. This can cause inconsistency and availability problems.
    • Updates at all locations. Any location can accept an update and forward it. Failures of replicas or updates can cause inconsistency.
    • Majority rules. An update is applied when a majority of locations agree.
  • Application-specific systems. Document stores include MongoDB and CouchDB. Graph stores include Neo4j and HypergraphDB.
Exam pointers:
  • Nested 2PC: a subtransaction whose ancestor aborts also aborts. Know the difference between hierarchical and flat 2PC.
  • Read-only optimisation: a subordinate that only sends READ VOTE writes no log and gets no second phase message.
  • ACID versus BASE: know the meaning of Basically Available, Soft state and Eventually consistent.
  • Know the three consistency policies (active location, all locations, majority) and their trade-offs.

Lecture 21: Google Bigtable and Amazon DynamoDB

Source: Lecture20-Databases3.pdf, slides 1–43

Note: the slide header prints "Lecture 21", but the file is named Lecture20-Databases3. The CAP theorem deck is also labelled Lecture 21. Treat the number on this deck as a slide typo.

Bigtable data model (slides 2–4)

A Bigtable is a sparse, distributed, persistent, multidimensional sorted map. Each value is addressed by a <Row, Column, Timestamp> triple. The API supports lookup, insert and delete. Columns are arbitrary and can differ from row to row. A column name has the form family:qualifier. A family is heavyweight and a qualifier is lightweight. The physical store is column-oriented, and the rows are sparse.

Bigtable is not a relational system. It has no table-wide integrity constraints and no multi-row transactions. Each cell can hold several timestamped versions.

Building blocks: SSTable, tablet, table (slides 4–6)

SSTable An immutable, sorted file of key-value pairs. It is made of 64 KB blocks plus an index. The index holds block ranges, not individual values. (The name stands for Sorted String Table.)
Tablet A contiguous range of rows of a table, built from several SSTables. Its start and end keys are given on the slide, for example aardvark to apple.
Table Several tablets together. Tablets never overlap, but SSTables can be shared between them and can overlap.

Bigtable keeps rows in lexicographic order by row key. The row range of a table is partitioned dynamically, so tablets split as data grows.

Servers and the master (slides 7–10)

A tablet server manages many tablets, but each tablet lives on exactly one server. A tablet is 100–200 MB. A tablet server splits a tablet that grows too large. The master does load balancing and fault handling. It also reassigns tablets from failed servers. Metadata changes are handled as follows. Tablet servers update the metadata directly when they split a tablet, then notify the master. The master may find out about a lost notification later, through lazy detection. The master also handles table creation and tablet merges.

The master uses Chubby, a lock service, to monitor servers. (background) Chubby is Google's distributed lock service that gives leases.

  • A tablet server registers itself by taking a lock in a specific Chubby directory. The lock comes with a lease that must be renewed periodically. A server that gets disconnected loses its lock.
  • The master watches that directory to see which servers are alive. If a server cannot be contacted or has lost its lock, the master takes the lock and reassigns the server's tablets.
  • GFS replicates the data, so the master prefers to start a tablet server on the machine where its data already sits.

When a new master starts, it does the following. It takes the master lock in Chubby, which ensures there is only one master at a time. It scans the Chubby directory to find live servers. It asks those servers which tablets they hold. It scans the metadata table to find all tablets, and it assigns any that are unassigned. The root of the metadata is read from Chubby, and the other metadata tablets are assigned before the scan.

Locating a tablet (slides 11–13)

Bigtable finds a tablet with a three-level hierarchy, similar to a B+-tree. The first level is a Chubby file that holds the location of the root tablet. The root tablet holds the locations of all tablets in a special METADATA table. Each METADATA tablet holds the locations of a set of user tablets. A METADATA row stores a tablet's location under a key made from the table identifier and the tablet's end row.

The slides give the sizing example. A METADATA row is about 1 KB in memory, and a METADATA tablet is 128 MB. So one tablet holds 128 M / 1 K = 217 entries. Three levels of this address 217 × 217 = 234 tablets.

Writes and compaction (slides 14–16)

Each edit is first appended to the tablet log in GFS, then applied to an in-memory memtable. Deletes are stored as special deletion entries. Updates are group-committed, so several are collected before the log is flushed.

  • Minor compaction. Turns the memtable into an SSTable. This frees memory and shortens the log that must be replayed on restart.
  • Merging compaction. Merges several SSTables into fewer. A natural place to enforce a policy such as "keep only N versions".
  • Major compaction. A merging compaction that leaves one SSTable with no deletion records, only live data.

Immutability. SSTables never change. This simplifies caching and sharing through GFS, and no concurrency control is needed on them. The master garbage-collects unused SSTables. When a tablet splits, the new tablets can start quickly on the shared SSTables and split them lazily. Only the memtable sees concurrent reads and writes. It uses copy-on-write rows so reads and writes can run together.

Consistency and availability of Bigtable (slide 17)

Bigtable always keeps data consistent, and this comes from using Chubby. The model is naturally partitioned by rows. The cost is availability. There can be brief downtimes when Chubby is unavailable or the network has problems.

Example applications (slides 18–19)

Google Analytics tracks traffic and site reports. Its raw click table is about 200 TB, with one row per end-user session. The row name combines the website name and the session creation time. Personalized Search records queries and clicks across web, image and news search. Each user has a row named by a unique user ID, and all of that user's actions are stored in one table.

Design space recap (slides 20–25)

These slides repeat the design-space points from the previous lecture: relational versus key-value data, levels of transaction support, replication and partitioning, the three consistency policies (active location, all locations, majority), and application-specific systems such as MongoDB, CouchDB, Neo4j and HypergraphDB.

DynamoDB overview (slides 26–29)

DynamoDB improves on SimpleDB, a simple key-value store. Dynamo is built for commodity hardware. It focuses on availability, scalability and reliability, and it keeps latency low for most requests, which matters for customer-facing applications. It is workload-aware. Most operations are simple key-value lookups, and no operation spans several data items. So it does not need the strong semantics of a relational model. It chooses availability over consistency.

Dynamo uses optimistic replication. Changes spread to replicas over time, writes are always accepted, even during partitions, and all replicas eventually converge. The hard questions are how to resolve conflicts and who resolves them. Applications can resolve conflicts using their own semantics. Otherwise Dynamo applies a simple policy such as "the latest write wins".

Dynamo architecture (slides 30–31)

Dynamo covers partitioning, load balancing, scalability, failure handling, replication, concurrency, routing and version management. The slide attaches a specific technique to three of them. Partitioning uses consistent hashing. Failure handling uses gossiping and quorum systems. Version management uses vector clocks.

The interface (slide 32)

There are two methods. get(key) returns an object, or a list of objects that have conflicting versions, together with a context. The context holds metadata such as the version. put(key, value, context) updates the key and its replicas, provided the context is still valid. Keys and values are byte arrays.

Partitioning with consistent hashing (slide 33)

Dynamo modifies basic consistent hashing. Each physical node is placed at several positions on the [0,1) ring, using several hash functions. Each position is a virtual node, and a physical node is a collection of one or more virtual nodes. Virtual nodes give better load balancing and support heterogeneous machines.

Replication and the preference list (slides 34–35)

Each object is stored at N replicas. The key k is stored at N nodes. The coordinator is the first node clockwise from h(k). The other N−1 replicas go to the next N−1 clockwise successors. If a successor is a virtual node of the coordinator, it is skipped, so that the N−1 replicas are distinct physical nodes. The list of distinct physical nodes that store an object is its preference list.

Versioning with vector clocks (slides 36–37)

Dynamo keeps several versions of an object at once. Newer versions usually subsume older ones. When updates happen concurrently or during failures, versions branch from a common ancestor. A vector clock is a set of (node, counter) pairs attached to each version. Comparing two vector clocks tells whether two versions are causally related. If they are not, they are conflicting. The application or Dynamo must then reconcile them.

Get and put with quorums (slides 38–41)

The node that handles a get or put is always the coordinator. Even if a request reaches a preference-list node that is not the coordinator, it is forwarded. Dynamo uses quorums with three parameters: N (replicas), R (read quorum size) and W (write quorum size). They must satisfy R + W > N.

  • Get. The coordinator asks all N nodes in the preference list for their versions and waits for at least R replies. It returns the versions that are not causally related. If there are several divergent versions, it reconciles them and writes back a reconciled version that supersedes them.
  • Put. The coordinator generates a vector timestamp for the put, writes the value locally, and sends the value and timestamp to the N−1 other nodes in the preference list. The write succeeds once the coordinator has acknowledgements from at least W−1 of them.

Failures during get and put (slide 42)

If the coordinator fails, the operation is handled by the highest-ranked node in the preference list. For a put, the update goes to the top N−1 reachable nodes in the preference list.

Choosing N, R and W (slide 43)

Small R and W give very high availability, but at the risk of more inconsistency. Large R and W can make the service unavailable at times. Most applications using Dynamo set N = 3 and R = W = 2. With N = 3 and R = W = 2, R + W = 4 > 3, so every read quorum overlaps every write quorum.

Exam pointers:
  • Bigtable location: a three-level hierarchy (Chubby file, root tablet, METADATA tablets). Be ready to redo the 217 and 234 arithmetic.
  • Bigtable write path: log, memtable, minor, merging and major compaction. Immutable SSTables.
  • Dynamo: consistent hashing with virtual nodes; preference list; coordinator is the node clockwise from h(k).
  • Quorums: R + W > N; N = 3, R = W = 2 is the common setting. Vector clocks detect concurrent (conflicting) versions.

Lecture 21: The CAP Theorem and Eventual Consistency

Source: Lecture21-CAPTheorem.pdf, slides 1–44

From ACID to BASE (slides 2–5)

RDBMSs follow ACID. NoSQL systems follow BASE, which the previous lecture introduced. Three guarantees matter from a user's point of view:

Consistency All replicas hold the same version of the data, and a client sees the same view no matter which node it talks to.
Availability The system keeps working when nodes fail, and every client can always read and write.
Partition tolerance The system keeps working across physical network partitions, and it has multiple entry points.

The question the slides raise is whether any system can have all three. The CAP theorem says no. In any distributed system, only two of the three properties can be guaranteed at once. The slides call this a fundamental limit.

The theorem and its origin (slides 6–9, 13)

Eric Brewer stated the observation in 2001. The slides paraphrase his point: if faults cannot be limited, and requests can go to any server while every request must be served, then the system cannot be consistent. Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch (MIT) proved a version of it in 2002. Their paper is "Brewer's conjecture and the feasibility of consistent, available, partition-tolerant web services".

The slides say why this matters. Relational databases are built on ACID, and a truly distributed relational database would need consistency, availability and partition tolerance together. The slides say that is impossible. Many design mistakes come from misunderstanding CAP.

Systems placed on the triangle (slide 7)

The slide lists DynamoDB, Cassandra, CouchDB and RDBMS on one side, and BigTable, MongoDB and HBase on the other. The text does not show which group sits at which corner, so the grouping is unclear.
