(background) The usual classification is AP for Dynamo, Cassandra and CouchDB, CP for BigTable, MongoDB and HBase, and CA for a single-node RDBMS. Check this against your lecture notes.

The "pick two" misconception (slides 16–21)

The slides first state the usual shorthand: pick two of C, A and P, which gives three kinds of system, CP, AP and CA. They then ask whether this is correct. Their answer is no. A CA system is not really possible on an unreliable network, because partitions cannot be avoided. The slides quote three practitioners:

  • Coda Hale: partition tolerance is mandatory in distributed systems, so you cannot choose not to have it.
  • Werner Vogels (Amazon CTO): in large systems partitions are a given, so consistency and availability cannot both be had at the same time.
  • Daniel Abadi: in reality there are two kinds of system. When a partition happens, the system gives up either availability or consistency.

Eric Brewer later wrote that the "2 of 3" formulation was always misleading. It oversimplifies the tensions. CAP only rules out perfect availability and consistency while partitions are happening, and partitions are rare.

Consistency and availability are not binary (slides 22–24)

The choice is not a switch. AP systems relax consistency for availability, but they are not inconsistent. CP systems give up availability for consistency, but they are not unavailable. Both can offer a degree of consistency and availability.

  • AP: best-effort consistency. Examples are web caching and DNS. They are optimistic and use expiry (time to live) and conflict resolution.
  • CP: best-effort availability. Examples are majority protocols and distributed locking, such as the Chubby lock service. They use pessimistic locking, and the minority partition becomes unavailable.

Types of consistency (slides 25–27)

Strong consistency After an update completes, every later access returns the updated value.
Weak consistency Later accesses are not guaranteed to return the updated value.
Eventual consistency A specific form of weak consistency. If no new updates are made, eventually all accesses return the last updated value. Updates reach replicas lazily.

Eventual consistency has several variations:

  • Causal consistency. Processes that are causally related see consistent data.
  • Read-your-writes. A process always sees its own update and never an older value.
  • Session consistency. Within one session, read-your-writes holds. Sessions do not overlap.
  • Monotonic reads. Once a process has seen a value, it never sees an older one.
  • Monotonic writes. The writes of one process are serialised.

In practice these are combined. The slides say monotonic reads and read-your-writes are the most desirable.

Examples of eventual consistency (slides 28–34)

Facebook. Bob posts a story on Alice's wall and asks her to check it. At first her wall is empty. After a minute it shows the story. Facebook uses an eventually consistent model. With more than a billion active users, storing all data reliably and strongly consistent is hard, and eventual consistency reduces load and improves availability.

Dropbox. Dropbox syncs immediately in many cases. During a partition it cannot be immediately consistent. The slides suggest an experiment: open a file, disconnect, edit, and reconnect. Dropbox chooses eventual consistency, because a Word document would freeze on every Ctrl+S if each save had to reach all devices across the WAN. Dropbox is built for personal sync rather than collaboration.

ATM. Strong consistency looks natural for a cash machine. In practice availability wins, because higher availability means higher revenue. An ATM can still dispense cash while partitioned from the network. It limits the amount you can withdraw, and the bank may charge an overdraft fee later.

Trading C against A dynamically (slide 35)

An airline reservation system can change its trade-off over time. When most seats are free, slightly stale data is fine and availability matters more. When the plane is nearly full, it needs more accurate data to avoid overbooking, so consistency matters more. The result is neither strong consistency nor guaranteed availability. It still tolerates network disruption much better.

Segmenting the system (slides 36–43)

There is no single requirement for the whole system. Some parts need strong consistency and others need high availability. The system can be split into components, each with its own guarantees, so each part gets what it needs. The overall service then offers neither strong consistency nor full availability. The slides list four ways to partition:

  • Data partitioning. A shopping cart can be highly available and occasionally anomalous. Product information can tolerate small inventory variations. Checkout, billing and shipping records must be consistent.
  • Operational partitioning. Reads (such as a query) favour availability. Writes (such as a purchase) favour consistency, using locks while writing.
  • Functional partitioning. A distributed lock service such as Chubby needs strong consistency, while DNS needs high availability.
  • User partitioning. Keep related data near its users, for example by running east-coast and west-coast data centres. A New York user querying a San Francisco server gets poorer performance.

The slides also mention hierarchical partitioning. In a large global service with local extensions, local servers are better connected and can guarantee more consistency and availability. Global servers see more partitions and relax one requirement.

Discussion (slides 37, 44)

The discussion asks students to design the trade-offs for an e-commerce site such as Amazon or Flipkart. The hints are to consider the type of data (cart, billing, product), the type of operation (query, purchase), the type of service (lock, DNS), and the group of users (by region). Slide 44 closes by asking whether any two-out-of-three can really be achieved, and it leaves that open.

Exam pointers:
  • State CAP precisely: under a partition you must choose between consistency and availability. Know that the "pick two" wording is a simplification the slides criticise.
  • Know the difference between AP and CP, with one example each (DNS or caching for AP; Chubby or majority protocols for CP).
  • Know the definitions of strong, weak and eventual consistency, and the variations: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, session consistency.
  • Be ready to justify a design with the partitioning types (data, operational, functional, user, hierarchical).

Lecture 22: Graph Model, BFS, Spanning Trees, Bellman-Ford, and MST

Source: Lecture22.pdf, slides 1–41

This lecture sets up the graph model for the rest of the module, then builds a set of algorithms: BFS, spanning trees, Bellman-Ford, broadcast and convergecast, and the GHS minimum spanning tree algorithm. For every algorithm, keep asking two questions: what does each node know at the start, and what does it do when a message arrives?

System model

The network is modelled as a graph G. Each processor is a node, and each communication link is an edge. Bidirectional links give an undirected graph; one-way links give a directed graph. The slides leave the topology arbitrary.

Nature of execution

Two axes classify distributed algorithms.

  • Centralized vs distributed. A centralized algorithm has asymmetric roles (client–server). It has processing and bandwidth bottlenecks and a single point of failure. A distributed algorithm gives nodes more balanced roles, but it is harder to design well. The slides cite snapshot algorithms and tree-based algorithms as examples.
  • Synchronous vs asynchronous. A synchronous model assumes three things: an upper bound on message delay, a known bound on how far each clock drifts from real time, and a known upper bound on how long a process takes to execute one logical step. An asynchronous model is one where these criteria are not satisfied. In practice there is a spectrum of models between the two. The algorithm you design depends heavily on which assumptions you pick.

Slide 6 makes a stronger point. Distributed systems are inherently asynchronous, so algorithms should ideally be designed for the asynchronous model. Most designers still work in the synchronous model because it is easier to reason about. A synchronizer is a construct that converts a synchronous algorithm into an asynchronous one.

Complexity measures

Sequential algorithms are measured by time, space and disk accesses. For distributed algorithms the slides list the following.

  • Space per node, and system-wide space.
  • Time per node, and system-wide time. The question here is whether nodes execute fully concurrently.
  • Message complexity, which has two parts: the number of messages, and the size of each message. The number affects space used by message overhead. The size affects overhead and transmission time.
  • Message time complexity, which depends on how many messages there are, how large they are, and how much sending and receiving happens at the same time.

Slide 9 adds counts of send and receive events and of multicasts. For shared-memory systems it adds the size of shared memory and the number of synchronization operations. These measures shift a little depending on the model.

Synchronous BFS

Assumptions: every node knows its neighbours, and a source (initiator) is known in advance. BFS arranges nodes into levels 0, 1, 2, …, so that a node at level i has a parent at level i − 1. The algorithm runs as follows.

  1. The initiator marks itself at level 0 and sends a QUERY, carrying its level, to all its neighbours.
  2. A neighbour that receives a QUERY marks itself at level 1 (the sender's level plus one) and sends its own QUERY onward.
  3. A node can receive several QUERYs in the same round. It may pick any of the senders as its parent and sets its level from that parent.
  4. The process repeats until every node has a valid level. A node can terminate once it has a level and has sent its QUERY messages.

The worked example on slide 15 uses node a as the source. Nodes b and d are marked in the round after the source, and the remaining nodes are marked in the third round. The extracted text has no edge list, so check the slide to see which parent each node picks.

The pseudo-code (Algorithm 18) is a clean version of this. Each node keeps a marked flag, a level and a parent. The source sends a mark message with level 1 to its neighbours. In each of D rounds, an unmarked node that receives a mark message records the sender as its parent, sets level to the sender's level plus one, and forwards its own mark message.

Complexity. Local space is O(degree), so global space is the sum of local space. Local time is O(diameter + degree). Each node sends at most two messages per edge. Each message carries a node ID, so its size is O(node id). The slides note that the algorithm can be modified so that each node also finds its children.

Asynchronous spanning tree

The main difficulty in the asynchronous setting is that a node cannot tell which of its neighbours will become its children. That uncertainty also makes it hard to decide when a node may terminate. The fix is to add two extra message types, ACCEPT and REJECT, on top of QUERY.

  • Once a node has a parent and a valid level, it floods QUERY to its other neighbours.
  • A node without a level accepts the sender of the first QUERY it gets as its parent, and sends ACCEPT to that parent.
  • Every later QUERY the node receives gets a REJECT.
  • A node can terminate only after it has replies (ACCEPT or REJECT) from every neighbour it sent a QUERY to.

The slides give the program in two parts. Part one covers the local variables (parent, Children, Unrelated, Neighbors) and the rules for starting the algorithm and handling QUERY. Part two covers the rules for ACCEPT and REJECT. Both use the same termination test: a node terminates when Children ∪ Unrelated equals Neighbors minus {parent}.

Complexity. Local space is the degree of the node, and global space is O(sum of local space). Local time is O(degree). Each edge carries between 2 and 4 messages, so the total is between 2l and 4l, where l is the number of links. Message time is d + 1 hops, where d is the diameter. The slides make no claim about the tree's height, except that the worst case is n − 1. Slide 23 is titled "Example – To do", so there is no worked example here.

Bellman-Ford for single-source shortest paths

Bellman-Ford can be run in a distributed setting with little change. The input is a weighted graph with no negative-weight cycles. No node has a global view and each knows only its local topology. The algorithm is synchronous, and each node is assumed to know n, the number of nodes, because that is what lets it decide when to stop.

The key invariant is this. After k rounds, the length stored at any node is the length of the shortest path to that node that uses at most k hops. After k rounds, the distances to all nodes at most k hops away along the final shortest-path tree have stabilized.

The pseudo-code runs as follows. The source sets its length to 0 and every other node sets its length to ∞. In each of n − 1 rounds, each node sends its current length to all neighbours (an UPDATE message). It then waits for an UPDATE from each neighbour. If going through neighbour j gives a shorter path, that is, length is greater than length_j + weight(j,i), the node updates its length and sets parent to j.

Complexity. The algorithm terminates after n − 1 rounds, so its time complexity is n − 1 rounds. The message complexity is (n − 1) · l, where l is the number of links.

Broadcast and convergecast (primitives)

Broadcast and convergecast are subroutines that many distributed algorithms reuse. Both run on a tree.

  • Broadcast distributes information from the root. BC1: the root sends the information to all its children, then terminates. BC2: a non-root node that receives the information from its parent copies it, forwards it to its children, and terminates.
  • Convergecast collects information at the root to compute a global function. CVC1: a leaf sends its report to its parent, then terminates. CVC2: a non-root, non-leaf node waits until it has a report from every child, sends the combined report to its parent, and terminates. CVC3: when the root has a report from every child, it evaluates the global function and terminates.

Uses include computing the minimum or maximum, leader election, and computing global state functions. Time is O(h), where h is the height of the tree. Both broadcast and convergecast use n − 1 messages.

The slides name cross and back edges in the figure but do not define them. (background) Non-tree edges of a depth-first-style spanning tree join a node to one of its ancestors (a back edge) or to a node in another branch (a cross edge).

Minimum spanning tree (GHS)

The problem: given a weighted connected graph on n nodes, find a spanning tree whose edge weights sum to the minimum. Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms do not work well in a distributed setting. The Gallager–Humblet–Spira (GHS) algorithm is the standard alternative.

MST fragment A connected subgraph F of the MST T.
Outgoing edge An edge with one endpoint in fragment F and the other outside F.
MOE (minimum-weight outgoing edge) The lightest outgoing edge of fragment F.

The slides ask you to check that the MOE of any fragment is an edge of the MST. This is what lets GHS add MOEs safely. (background) It follows from the cut property: the lightest edge crossing a cut belongs to the MST.

GHS runs in phases. At the start, every node is its own fragment. All fragments find their MOEs in parallel, and then merge along them. After enough phases, a single fragment remains, and it is the MST. Each fragment keeps a leader, which is its root. Every node knows its parent and children, and every fragment is identified by its root's ID (the fragment ID).

A phase has two steps.

  1. Find the MOE. The root broadcasts <Find MOE> down the fragment. Each node checks its incident edges to find its lightest outgoing edge. The nodes then convergecast these candidates to the root, which takes the minimum.
  2. Merge. The root broadcasts <Merge MOE>. The node that has the MOE sends a "Request to combine" to the node at the other end. When two fragments choose the same edge, the node with the higher identifier becomes the root of the combined fragment. That root broadcasts <NEW-FRAGMENT> through the fragment edges and the chosen MOE edges, and every node updates its parent, children and fragment ID.

The slide notes that each fragment has only one outgoing MOE, so at most one pair of neighbouring nodes can be merging through the same edge in one step.

Analysis of GHS

  • Each phase at least halves the number of fragments, so there are O(log n) phases.
  • Each phase takes O(n) time, since all messages travel along the MST, whose diameter is at most O(n).
  • Each phase uses O(n) messages for merging, plus the messages needed to find MOEs. Over the whole run this is O(m + n log n) messages, because each node checks its neighbours in increasing weight order, starting from the last one it checked, so each edge is checked only once. (background: this is the amortization argument.)

Final result. GHS computes a distributed MST in O(n log n) rounds using O(m + n log n) messages.

Later advances: a pipelined algorithm runs in O(n) time using O(n²) messages. The Garay–Kutten–Peleg algorithm runs GHS in a controlled way, so the number of fragments still at least halves each phase while the fragment diameter grows only by a constant factor. Once the diameter is within O(√n), it switches to the pipelined algorithm.

Exam pointers:
  • Bellman-Ford: after k rounds a node holds the shortest path using at most k hops. It takes n − 1 rounds and (n − 1) · l messages. Each node must know n.
  • Asynchronous spanning tree: ACCEPT and REJECT solve the problem of not knowing children. Messages are between 2l and 4l, and the worst-case height is n − 1.
  • Broadcast and convergecast each use n − 1 messages and O(h) time on a tree of height h.
  • GHS: know the definitions of fragment, outgoing edge and MOE. The fragment count halves per phase, giving O(log n) phases, and the final bounds are O(n log n) rounds and O(m + n log n) messages.

Lecture 23: Maximal Independent Sets, Luby's Algorithm, Leader Election, and Model Taxonomy

Source: Lecture23.pdf, slides 1–42

Slides 1–27 cover MIS, Luby's randomized algorithm, and leader election. Slides 28–42 are headed "Lecture 24" in the deck, but their content is taxonomy and computation models (LOCAL, CONGEST, CONGESTED-CLIQUE), so they are included here.

Quick recap

Earlier lectures covered distributed graph algorithms: BFS, asynchronous spanning trees, shortest paths, the convergecast and broadcast primitives, and MST.

Maximal independent sets (MIS)

An independent set U is a set of vertices with no edge between any two of them. U is maximal if no proper superset of U is also independent, so no vertex outside U can be added. Maximal is not the same as maximum. A graph can have several maximal independent sets of different sizes, and the largest one is the maximum independent set.

MIS An independent set that cannot be extended by adding any vertex.

The slides give wireless broadcast as an application. Nodes that interfere with each other cannot share a frequency band, so an MIS gives a set of transmitters that can all use the same band at once. The slides label the problem NP-complete without saying which version. (background) Finding a maximum independent set is NP-hard, but finding some MIS is easy to do sequentially, as the greedy method below shows.

Greedy sequential algorithm

GreedyMIS: start with U empty and S = V. While S is not empty, pick a vertex v in S, add v to U, and remove v and all of its neighbours from S. Return U. This always gives an MIS, and it is very easy to design. The problem is that it is sequential: each choice depends on the earlier ones, so it can take a long time in a distributed system.

What a distributed algorithm needs is a quick way to separate neighbours, so that no two neighbours both join the MIS. This is called symmetry breaking. The slides say that deterministic algorithms need nearly n rounds in the worst case. Randomization is what makes the problem tractable.

Luby's algorithm

Each node is in one of two states, active or inactive. All nodes start active. In each round:

  1. Each active node v picks a random bit. It picks 1 with probability 1/(2d(v)) and 0 otherwise. A 1 means v wants to join the MIS. (The slide text is garbled here as "½ d(v)". Claim 1 on slide 14 makes clear the probability is 1/(2d(v)).)
  2. Each node that picked 1 tells its active neighbours.
  3. A node that picked 1 withdraws from the contest if a neighbour of higher degree also picked 1. A withdrawing node stays active for now.
  4. An active node that picked 1 and did not withdraw joins the MIS and becomes inactive. It tells its active neighbours.
  5. Any active node with a neighbour that just joined the MIS becomes inactive.

The randomness is what breaks symmetry. A low-degree node is more likely to win, so the high-degree neighbours of a low-degree node tend to drop out. The slides say this is not obvious from the rules alone, and that the analysis is needed to see the benefit.

Result. Luby's algorithm finishes in O(log n) rounds with high probability. The argument is that in each round a constant fraction of the edges become redundant. An edge is redundant once either of its endpoints is inactive. So after O(log n) rounds, every edge is redundant.

Analysis of Luby's algorithm

The analysis uses four definitions.

  • A vertex v is good if more than 1/3 of its neighbours have degree less than d(v).
  • A vertex v is bad if at least 2/3 of its neighbours have degree at least d(v).
  • An edge is good if at least one of its endpoints is good.
  • An edge is bad if both of its endpoints are bad.

The sketch: a good vertex has enough low-degree neighbours. Low-degree neighbours are more likely to be marked, and a marked low-degree neighbour is likely to join the MIS. That in turn makes v inactive. If enough edges are good, then deleting a fraction of the good edges is enough.

Claim 1. For a good vertex v with d(v) > 0, the probability that some neighbour w of v gets marked is at least 1 − e−1/6. Proof sketch: at least d(v)/3 neighbours have degree at most d(v). Each such w is marked with probability 1/(2d(w)) ≥ 1/(2d(v)). So the probability that none of them is marked is at most (1 − 1/(2d(v)))d(v)/3 ≤ e−1/6. This bound ignores what high-degree neighbours do, which only helps.

Claim 2. If a vertex w is marked, then Pr(w ∈ S) ≥ 1/2. Proof sketch: w fails to join only if some high-degree neighbour u is also marked. Each such u is marked with probability at most 1/(2d(w)), and there are at most d(w) of them. A union bound gives 1 − d(w) · 1/(2d(w)) = 1/2.

Claim 3. For a good vertex v, Pr(v is deleted) ≥ (1 − e−1/6)/2. This follows by combining Claims 1 and 2.

Claim 4. At least half of the edges are good. Proof sketch: orient each edge towards its higher-degree endpoint. For a bad edge e = (u, v) oriented towards v, v is bad, so its out-degree is at least twice its in-degree. That lets us assign to each bad edge a pair of edges, and the assignment is injective on pairs of distinct bad edges. There are only |E|/2 such disjoint pairs, so at most half the edges are bad. The slide has the full construction.

Putting it together. In each iteration, half the edges are good, and each good edge is deleted with probability at least (1 − e−1/6)/2. So a constant fraction of edges is removed in expectation. This gives O(log m) = O(log n) iterations in expectation, and O(log n) iterations with high probability.

Leader election

Given a (directed) graph G = (V, E), one node must be designated as the leader. The slides mention that the two-phase commit algorithm, covered earlier, depends on leader election.

Ring. The simplest case is a bidirectional ring. Each process can tell its clockwise neighbour from its counter-clockwise neighbour. The algorithm is:

  • Each process sends its UID around the ring.
  • On receiving a UID, compare it with your own. If it is larger, pass it on. If it is smaller, discard it. If it is equal, declare yourself leader.

Correctness is shown by induction on the number of rounds r. After r rounds, the node that is r hops away from the maximum-UID process starts sending UIDmax. When r = n, UIDmax has travelled all the way round the ring, and the maximum node receives its own UID and declares itself leader. The slide's ring has five processes with UIDs from 1 to 5. (background) This simple algorithm takes O(n) rounds, but it can send O(n²) messages in the worst case.

Hirshberg–Sinclair improvement. The slide spells the name "Hirshberg". The algorithm works in phases. In phase p, each candidate sends its UID in both directions for a distance that the slide writes as 2p. A UID that comes back unchanged lets the process continue to the next phase. If a process gets its own UID back, it declares itself leader. The slide gives the result as O(n log n) communication and O(n) time. (background) The standard algorithm uses distance 2p, not 2p, and it is the doubling that gives the O(n log n) message bound. Check your course notes before using the exact distance in an answer.

General graphs: FloodMax. Each process keeps the largest UID it has seen. In each round, it sends that UIDmax on all outgoing links. After diam rounds, a process whose UIDmax is its own UID declares itself leader. The communication cost is diam · |E|, where |E| counts outgoing edges.

Terminology

  • Synchronous vs asynchronous is one classification. Other categories exist, and they often overlap.
  • Uniform algorithms do not use any knowledge of the graph's topology: not n, diameter, number of links, or degree. They scale naturally, because a change in the input needs no change to the algorithm. The slides note that a rule such as "pick an action with a probability based on degree" is not uniform, since a change in the graph changes the degree.
  • Symmetric algorithms have all nodes performing similar roles. Luby's algorithm is symmetric. A source-initiated BFS is asymmetric, because the source plays a different role.
  • Anonymous algorithms use no node identifiers. They are usually very hard to design, and many problems have been shown impossible in this setting. Most algorithms use IDs to break ties.

Models for distributed algorithms

The slides list four models: LOCAL, CONGEST, CONGESTED-CLIQUE, and the Massively Parallel Computing model (covered in the MPC material).

LOCAL model

Each round consists of local computation and sending and receiving messages. Local computation is ignored in the complexity, however costly it is. Message size is also ignored: a node can send a message of any size polynomial in the input size to each neighbour in one round. Efficiency is measured by the number of rounds.

For most graph problems, the diameter gives a trivial upper bound. Every node sends its neighbour list to node 1, which assembles the graph, solves the problem, and sends the answer back to everyone. Better algorithms exist for many problems. For MIS, the slide gives a randomized bound of roughly √(log n) times a second logarithmic term, but the exact expression is garbled in the extracted text.

A common technique for fast algorithms is to run a simple, slow algorithm for a few rounds, and then analyse the progress it has made. That gives bounds on the leftover graph. Because message size is unlimited in LOCAL, the leftover graph can be gathered at one node, solved locally, and the answer sent back out. Lower bounds are much harder to prove, and only a few are known.

CONGEST model

The network is again a graph, with nodes as processes and edges as links. The departure from LOCAL is that link bandwidth is limited. Messages have a bounded size, and larger messages take more rounds. The bandwidth is usually O(log n) bits per link, where n is the number of nodes. That is the number of bits needed to send one node ID, so the limit is not artificial.

Non-trivial lower bounds are not known for many problems, and algorithms are harder to design than in LOCAL. Luby's MIS algorithm can be made to run in CONGEST.

CONGESTED-CLIQUE model

This model is quite different from LOCAL and CONGEST. The communication network is a clique: every pair of n nodes has a link. The input graph is a spanning subgraph of this clique, so it has the same n nodes but possibly fewer links. All clique links can be used to solve the problem, even those that are not input edges. Each link has a bandwidth of O(log n) bits. It is an all-to-all communication model. The extra links let information move quickly, but the message size per round is still limited.

Open issues

  • The slides say CONGESTED-CLIQUE is a bit too relaxed and artificial, because building a clique is not practical at scale.
  • Expanders are a more realistic option. An expander has good connectivity between any two subsets of n/2 nodes.
  • Expanders with low degree, even constant degree O(1), exist.
Exam pointers:
  • MIS is about symmetry breaking. Luby's algorithm joins with probability 1/(2d(v)) and finishes in O(log n) rounds with high probability.
  • Know the good and bad definitions. Claim 3 gives the deletion probability (1 − e−1/6)/2 for a good vertex.
  • Ring leader election compares UIDs and takes O(n) rounds. Hirshberg–Sinclair gives O(n log n) messages.
  • FloodMax runs for diam rounds and costs diam · |E| communication.
  • Models: LOCAL ignores message size, CONGEST allows O(log n) bits per link per round, and CONGESTED-CLIQUE lets every pair of nodes communicate.

Lecture 24: The Massively Parallel Computing (MPC) Model, Sorting, and MST

Source: Lecture24.pdf, slides 1–27

The LOCAL and CONGEST models measure rounds of communication between nodes of a graph. The MPC model is closer to a cloud cluster: many machines, each with limited memory, and no machine can hold the whole input. This lecture defines MPC, then works through two algorithms, sorting and MST, and finishes with the regimes that depend on memory per machine.

Why MPC

The slides say it is important to connect distributed computing models to practical ones such as the cloud. MPC is one step in that direction. It has a set of machines, all pairwise interconnected. The key assumption is that no single machine can store the entire input. Space is not enough, so the question becomes how many rounds of communication are needed.

The MPC model

  • The input has size N. Each machine has space S, with N ≫ S.
  • In each round, a machine can send and receive up to S units of data over its links.
  • The input is spread evenly over O(N/S) machines, each holding O(S) data.
  • A round is one local computation followed by communication (send and receive).
  • The measure of efficiency is the number of communication rounds. Communication is usually slower than computation, so focusing on rounds is reasonable.

A first MPC algorithm: sorting

Suppose we have m machines, each with space S, and N items to sort. Assume S = Nδ for a constant δ > 1/2. (The exponent symbol is partly lost in the extracted text, so read the constant as δ.) The algorithm resembles quicksort, except that it uses many pivots at once. The steps are as follows.

  1. Choose pivots. Let Ni be the set of numbers on machine Mi, and let ni = |Ni|. Each machine picks each of its elements as a pivot with probability p. So it picks about ni · p pivots.
  2. Share pivots. Each machine sends its chosen pivots to every other machine.
  3. Compute local ranks. Each machine computes the local rank of every pivot q: Rank(q, i) is the number of elements in Mi smaller than q. Each machine sends these local ranks to a designated machine M.
  4. Select global pivots. M uses the local ranks to estimate global ranks. It picks a set Q of pivots, about one for every block of N input elements. M sends Q to all machines.
  5. Partition. Each machine splits its input into |Q| + 1 buckets. Bucket j holds the values between the (j − 1)th and j-th pivot. Set q0 = −∞ and q|Q|+1 = ∞.
  6. Exchange. In a final round, each machine sends each element x with qj−1 ≤ x < qj to machine Mj. Machine Mj then holds exactly the values between two consecutive pivots.
  7. Sort locally. Mj sorts its values, and gives them global ranks starting just after the global rank of qj−1.

Analysis of the sorting algorithm

There are two requirements on p. There must not be too many pivots, and there must be a pivot in every block of N ranks.

Lemma. With high probability, some machine marks at least one element in every segment of N ranks of the input. Proof: the probability that no machine marks any element in a given segment of N ranks is (1 − p)N ≤ exp(−pN). Setting pN = 4 log N makes this exp(−4 log N) = N−4, which is O(1/N4). (The extracted text reads "4S log N", but the calculation only works with 4 log N.) A union bound over the blocks then gives the lemma.

Communication rounds. Each machine selects O(ni · p) pivots with high probability. The total number of words a machine receives is O(N · p). Set p so that N · p = S, that is, p = S/N. Then the communication volume at each machine is O(S). The last step, which moves the elements to their buckets, also has volume O(S). So the algorithm needs only a constant number of rounds.

Observations. The slides point out that the number of machines and the space per machine trade off against each other. No single machine ever looks at every element of the input. The design principle is to find mechanisms that let each machine do its job without routing the whole input to every machine. The same ideas give O(1)-round MPC algorithms for frequency estimates and prefix sums. MapReduce has a sort function that does something similar to this.

MPC for graphs

A graph G = (V, E) with |V| = n and |E| = m has input size O(n + m). The relationship between the memory per machine S and n determines the regime.

  • Superlinear: S = n1+ε for a constant ε > 0.
  • Linear: S = Θ(n).
  • Sublinear: S = O(n1−ε) for a constant ε > 0. (The slides give the same regime as S = O(nδ) for 0 < δ < 1 on slide 20.)

Strongly superlinear regime

Here S = O(n1+ε) for 0 < ε < 1. A machine has space for more than all n vertices. For the model to be realistic, the graph must be dense, with m ≫ S ≫ n. The slides stress that even though the input is dense, each machine's O(n1+ε) memory makes the model powerful.

Near-linear regime

Here S = Õ(n). Each machine can store O(n) information. Most graph algorithms need more rounds here than in the strongly superlinear regime.

Strongly sublinear regime

Here S is a small power of n, so no machine can store even one piece of information about every vertex. Most graph algorithms have higher round complexity in this regime.

Super-linear MST

In the super-linear regime, each machine has space S = n1+ε, so it can store all vertices and more. The MST algorithm uses that extra space. Let m = n1+c for a constant 0 < c < 1. The slides note that c must exceed ε, otherwise the problem is easy to solve.

  1. Partition the edges of G into E1, E2, …, Er, with |Ei| = n1+ε.
  2. Compute Ti = MST(Ei) on each machine.
  3. Recursively compute the MST of the union of the Ti, and return that result.

Why is this correct? The key lemma is a filtering lemma. Let F be a subset of the edges, and let G′ be the subgraph spanned by F. If an edge e ∈ F is not in the MST (or minimum spanning forest) of G′, then e is not in the MST of G. The proof uses the cycle property: the heaviest edge on a cycle is never in the MST. If e is not in the MSF of G′, then e is the heaviest edge on some cycle C of G′. C is also a cycle in G, since G′ is a subgraph of G, so e is still the heaviest edge on C in G, and it cannot be in the MST of G.

So each step can throw away edges that cannot be in the MST. The count works as follows. The number of partitions is m/n1+ε = nc−ε, which is also the number of machines. After one iteration, the number of edges left in ∪Ti is at most nc−ε × n = n1+c−ε, since each Ti has at most n edges. Each further recursive call reduces the edge count from n1+c−ε to n1+c−2ε, and so on. After (c/ε) − 1 recursive calls, at most n1+ε edges remain, and they fit on one machine. So the algorithm takes O(1/ε) rounds.

In the pseudo-code, the constant is written as c = 4. That is a divisor in the chunk size, and it is not the same c as the exponent in m = n1+c. The two uses are easy to confuse.

Summary

The lecture covers two MPC algorithms: sorting and MST. The slides say progress on MPC algorithms has been much more pronounced in the last decade, and that many graph problems have very efficient MPC algorithms in all memory regimes.

Exam pointers:
  • Sorting uses p = S/N, so each machine's communication is O(S) per round. The high-probability argument uses pN = 4 log N.
  • Know the four memory regimes and how S relates to n in each: superlinear, near-linear, linear, and sublinear.
  • MST filtering lemma: an edge that is not in the MSF of a subgraph is not in the MST of G. This follows from the cycle property.
  • Super-linear MST runs in O(1/ε) rounds. Each round shrinks the edge count from n1+c−kε until it fits on one machine.

Lecture 25: Termination Detection

Source: Lecture25.pdf, slides 1–37

Termination detection asks a simple question: has a distributed computation finished? The difficulty is that no process knows the global state, and there is no global clock. This lecture defines the problem, gives a snapshot-based algorithm, then a spanning-tree algorithm, and finally a message-optimal variant.

The problem

A computation can consist of several distributed subprograms. They may not run on the same machine, and there can be dependencies between them. For example, subprogram SP2 must finish before SP5 can start. Every processor then needs to know whether SP2 and SP4 have finished, so that SP5 can start.

Globally terminated A distributed computation is globally terminated if every process is locally terminated and there is no message in transit between any two processes.
Locally terminated A process has finished its computation and will not restart any action unless it receives a message.

In the termination detection problem, one process (or all of them) must infer when the underlying computation has terminated. The slides stress that this is non-trivial, because no process has complete knowledge of the global state and global time does not exist.

Conditions a termination detection algorithm must satisfy

  1. Running the termination detection (TD) algorithm must not indefinitely delay the underlying computation.
  2. The TD algorithm must not require new communication channels between processes.

Most TD algorithms use two kinds of messages. Basic messages belong to the underlying computation. Control messages exist only to detect termination.

System assumptions

  • At any time, a process is in one of two states: active or idle.
  • An active process is doing local computation. It can become idle at any time.
  • An idle process has finished its local computation. It can become active again only on receiving a message from another process.
  • Only active processes can send messages.
  • A process can receive a message in either state. On receiving one, an idle process becomes active.

Characterizing termination

Let pi(t) be the state of process pi at instant t. Let ci,j(t) be the number of messages in transit on the channel from pi to pj at instant t. The computation has terminated at time t0 if and only if

(∀i: pi(t0) = idle) ∧ (∀i, j: ci,j(t0) = 0).

In words: every process is idle, and no channel holds a message. Both conditions must hold at the same instant. Idle processes alone are not enough, because a message in transit would wake one of them.

Termination detection via distributed snapshots

The algorithm assumes a logical bidirectional channel between every pair of processes. Channels are reliable but can deliver messages in arbitrary order. Message delay is arbitrary but finite. The idea is to use snapshot requests and snapshots to infer termination.

Main idea. When a process goes from active to idle, it asks every other process to take a local snapshot. It also takes one itself. A process that receives the request grants it, by taking a snapshot, if it agrees that the requester became idle after it did. A request succeeds if every process has taken a local snapshot for it. The requester, or any external agent, can collect those snapshots. If a request succeeds, the global snapshot shows that the computation has terminated.

Formal details

  • Each process i keeps a logical clock x, starting at zero. It increments x each time it becomes idle.
  • B(x) is a basic message sent at logical time x.
  • R(x, i) is a control message requesting a local snapshot, issued by process i at its logical time x.
  • Clocks follow the scalar-time rules. The current time is the maximum of all clock values ever sent or received.
  • Each process also keeps k = max_j Req_Snapshot(x, j), the largest request tuple it has seen.

Requests are tuples (x, j), compared in lexicographic order: (x, j) > (x′, j′) if x > x′, or if x = x′ and j > j′. For example, (4, 5) < (5, 3), and (6, 7) > (6, 2). Process IDs break ties.

The four rules

  1. R1 (send). An active process i may send a basic message B(x) to j at any time.
  2. R2 (receive basic message). On receiving B(x′), process i sets x := max(x, x′) + 1. If i is idle, it becomes active.
  3. R3 (go idle). When process i goes idle, it sets x := x + 1 and k := i. It sends Req_Snapshot(x, k) to all other processes, and takes a local snapshot for that request.
  4. R4 (receive snapshot request). On receiving Req_Snapshot(x′, k′): if i is active, it sets x := max(x′, x). If (x′, k′) > (x, k) and i is idle, it sets (x, k) := (x′, k′) and takes a local snapshot for that request. If (x′, k′) ≤ (x, k) and i is idle, it does nothing.

Intuition. The last process to terminate has the largest clock value. Every process will therefore take a snapshot for its request, and the snapshots together show that all processes were idle with no messages in transit. Rule R4 says that an idle process only answers requests that are newer than the last one it answered.

Cost. The slides warn that the algorithm can be quite costly in messages. They ask what the worst case could be, but do not answer it on the slide. The next algorithm uses a spanning tree to reduce this cost.

Termination detection via spanning trees

This approach does not need several snapshots. The N processes are arranged in a logical spanning tree. P0 is the root and is responsible for detecting termination. The slides assume synchronous communication for this algorithm. Each leaf reports to its parent when it has terminated. A parent reports to its own parent once it has finished and all its children have terminated. The root concludes that termination has occurred when it has terminated and all its immediate children have terminated.

A first attempt, and why it fails

Each leaf starts with a token. When a leaf terminates, it sends its token to its parent. When a parent has terminated and has received a token from each child, it sends a token to its own parent. So each process tells its parent that its subtree is idle. The root decides that termination has occurred once it is idle and has received a token from each child.

The slides point out the flaw. A process that reported idle to its parent can become active again, because a message to an idle process reactivates it. So an idle report is not a permanent fact. A token can be wrong, and the root may then declare termination incorrectly. The root cannot conclude from a child's token alone that the child's subtree has terminated.

Fixing the first attempt

The fix needs two things. First, signals must show that a message may be in transit while some process has already declared local termination. Second, the root must not declare termination immediately. It must verify the claim.

The algorithm works with two waves of signals. A contracting wave of tokens moves inward from the leaves to the root. If the token wave reaches the root without detecting termination, the root starts a second, outward wave of repeat signals. As the repeat wave reaches the leaves, a new token wave forms and moves inward again. This cycle repeats until termination is detected.

Setup. Each leaf is given a token. The set S records which processes hold a token, and at the start S is the set of all leaves. All processes and tokens are coloured white.

Colouring rules.

  • A process turns black when it sends a message to some other process.
  • When a process terminates, if it is black, it sends a black token to its parent. A black process turns white again after it has sent a black token.
  • A parent that holds a black token from any child sends only a black token to its own parent. A black token means that a message was passed somewhere in its subtree.

Restart. The root, on receiving a black token, knows that some process in the tree sent a message. So it restarts the algorithm by sending a Repeat signal to all its children. Each child passes Repeat to its children, and so on until it reaches the leaves. Each leaf restarts the algorithm on receiving Repeat.

Declaration. The root concludes that termination has occurred if all three conditions hold:

  1. it is white,
  2. it is idle, and
  3. it has received a white token from each of its children.

Message complexity

  • Best case: O(N) messages, where N is the number of processes. This happens when all nodes send all their computation messages in the first round.
  • Worst case: O(N · M), where M is the number of computation messages. This happens when the root has to restart detection M times.

The algorithm is expensive in the worst case because it does not choose well when to restart. Not every message should trigger a restart. The next algorithm addresses this.

Message-optimal termination detection

This algorithm assumes three things: FIFO message delivery, a spanning tree of the processes, and a leader.

The problem it fixes. Suppose node q has already sent a white token to its parent before a message m from p arrives. When m arrives, q becomes active. But p cannot send a white token to its own parent until q is idle again. The old algorithm handles this by making p black and sending a black token, which triggers another round of detection.

The optimisation. If process p sends a message to q, p should wait until q becomes idle. For this, q sends an acknowledgement to p once q's actions caused by p's message are complete. The acknowledgement tells p that it can now send a white token to its parent.

  • The idea can recurse. If q wakes an idle process r, q waits for an acknowledgement from r before it acknowledges p.
  • In general, a node sends a white token only after it has received an acknowledgement for every message it sent, and a white token from every child.

The slides say this can be developed into an algorithm that is optimal in messages. It keeps a stack of acknowledgements still to be received, and the details are in the textbook.

Other variants

Other variants change the rule for leaving the idle state. In some, a process goes active only on receiving a message from a specific set of processes. For example, P turns active only when it receives messages from Q1, Q2 and Q3 (all of them), or from Q1 or Q2 or Q3 (any of them), or from k out of n processes. A variant can also require that a predicate be true before a process becomes active. The termination detection logic has to be adapted to each such rule.

Exam pointers:
  • The termination condition: every process idle and every channel empty, at the same instant.
  • Snapshot rules R1 to R4. The last process to terminate has the largest (x, k), so its snapshot request is granted by everyone.
  • Spanning-tree flaw: an idle report can be undone by a later message. The fix is two waves, black and white tokens, and a root that checks for white, idle, and white tokens from each child.
  • Message cost: O(N) best case, O(N · M) worst case.
  • Message-optimal version: FIFO delivery, a tree, and acknowledgements before sending a white token.
